source.translation: On the authority of Amir al-Mu'minin, Abu Hafs Umar bin al-Khattab (ra), who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Actions are (judged) by motives (niyyah), so each man will have what he intended. source.arabic: عَنْ عُمَرَ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ أَيْضًا قَالَ: "بَيْنَمَا نَحْنُ جُلُوسٌ عِنْدَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم ذَاتَ يَوْمٍ، إذْ طَلَعَ عَلَيْنَا رَجُلٌ شَدِيدُ بَيَاضِ الثِّيَابِ، شَدِيدُ سَوَادِ الشَّعْرِ، لَا يُرَى عَلَيْهِ أَثَرُ السَّفَرِ، وَلَا يَعْرِفُهُ مِنَّا أَحَدٌ. حَتَّى جَلَسَ إلَى النَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه و سلم. فَأَسْنَدَ رُكْبَتَيْهِ إلَى رُكْبَتَيْهِ، وَوَضَعَ كَفَّيْهِ عَلَى فَخِذَيْهِ، وَقَالَ: يَا مُحَمَّدُ أَخْبِرْنِي عَنْ الْإِسْلَامِ. فَقَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم الْإِسْلَامُ أَنْ تَشْهَدَ أَنْ لَا إلَهَ إلَّا اللَّهُ وَأَنْ مُحَمَّدًا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ، وَتُقِيمَ الصَّلَاةَ، وَتُؤْتِيَ الزَّكَاةَ، وَتَصُومَ رَمَضَانَ، وَتَحُجَّ الْبَيْتَ إنْ اسْتَطَعْت إلَيْهِ سَبِيلًا. قَالَ: صَدَقْت. فَعَجِبْنَا لَهُ يَسْأَلُهُ وَيُصَدِّقُهُ! قَالَ: فَأَخْبِرْنِي عَنْ الْإِيمَانِ. قَالَ: أَنْ تُؤْمِنَ بِاَللَّهِ وَمَلَائِكَتِهِ وَكُتُبِهِ وَرُسُلِهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ، وَتُؤْمِنَ بِالْقَدَرِ خَيْرِهِ وَشَرِّهِ. قَالَ: صَدَقْت. قَالَ: فَأَخْبِرْنِي عَنْ الْإِحْسَانِ. قَالَ: أَنْ تَعْبُدَ اللَّهَ كَأَنَّك تَرَاهُ، فَإِنْ لَمْ تَكُنْ تَرَاهُ فَإِنَّهُ يَرَاك. قَالَ: فَأَخْبِرْنِي عَنْ السَّاعَةِ. قَالَ: مَا الْمَسْئُولُ عَنْهَا بِأَعْلَمَ مِنْ السَّائِلِ. قَالَ: فَأَخْبِرْنِي عَنْ أَمَارَاتِهَا؟ قَالَ: أَنْ تَلِدَ الْأَمَةُ رَبَّتَهَا، وَأَنْ تَرَى الْحُفَاةَ الْعُرَاةَ الْعَالَةَ رِعَاءَ الشَّاءِ يَتَطَاوَلُونَ فِي الْبُنْيَانِ. ثُمَّ انْطَلَقَ، فَلَبِثْتُ مَلِيًّا، ثُمَّ قَالَ: يَا عُمَرُ أَتَدْرِي مَنْ السَّائِلُ؟ قُلْتُ: اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ أَعْلَمُ. قَالَ: فَإِنَّهُ جِبْرِيلُ أَتَاكُمْ يُعَلِّمُكُمْ دِينَكُمْ".

Also on the authority of Umar (ra), who said: While we were one day sitting with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) there appeared before us a man with extremely white garments and extremely black hair. No signs of journeying were visible on him, and none of us knew him. He sat down by the Prophet (ﷺ) and leaned his knees against his, and placed his palms on his thighs, and said: 'O Muhammad, inform me about Islam'

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Islam is to testify that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, to perform the prayers, to pay the zakat, to fast in Ramadan, and to perform the pilgrimage to the House if you are able to find a way to it.' He said: 'You have spoken truthfully.' We were astonished at him, that he should ask him and then confirm his truthfulness!

He said: 'Then inform me about Iman.' He (ﷺ) said: 'It is to believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day, and to believe in qadar (divine decree), both the good and the evil of it.' He said: 'You have spoken truthfully.'

He said: 'Then inform me about Ihsan.' He (ﷺ) said: 'It is to worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then surely He sees you.'

He said: 'Then inform me about the Hour.' He (ﷺ) said: 'The one questioned about it knows no more than the questioner.' He said: 'Then inform me about its signs.' He said: 'That the slave-girl will give birth to her mistress, and that you will see the barefooted, naked, destitute herdsmen competing in making lofty buildings.' Then he departed and I stayed for a while. Then he (ﷺ) said to me: 'O Umar, do you know who the questioner was?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'He was Jibril (Gabriel), who came to teach you your religion.'

source.arabic: عَنْ أَبِي عَبْدِ الرَّحْمَنِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ مَسْعُودٍ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: حَدَّثَنَا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم -وَهُوَ الصَّادِقُ الْمَصْدُوقُ-: "إنَّ أَحَدَكُمْ يُجْمَعُ خَلْقُهُ فِي بَطْنِ أُمِّهِ أَرْبَعِينَ يَوْمًا نُطْفَةً، ثُمَّ يَكُونُ عَلَقَةً مِثْلَ ذَلِكَ، ثُمَّ يَكُونُ مُضْغَةً مِثْلَ ذَلِكَ، ثُمَّ يُرْسَلُ إلَيْهِ الْمَلَكُ فَيَنْفُخُ فِيهِ الرُّوحَ، وَيُؤْمَرُ بِأَرْبَعِ كَلِمَاتٍ: بِكَتْبِ رِزْقِهِ، وَأَجَلِهِ، وَعَمَلِهِ، وَشَقِيٍّ أَمْ سَعِيدٍ؛ فَوَاَللَّهِ الَّذِي لَا إلَهَ غَيْرُهُ إنَّ أَحَدَكُمْ لَيَعْمَلُ بِعَمَلِ أَهْلِ الْجَنَّةِ حَتَّى مَا يَكُونُ بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَهَا إلَّا ذِرَاعٌ فَيَسْبِقُ عَلَيْهِ الْكِتَابُ فَيَعْمَلُ بِعَمَلِ أَهْلِ النَّارِ فَيَدْخُلُهَا. وَإِنَّ أَحَدَكُمْ لَيَعْمَلُ بِعَمَلِ أَهْلِ النَّارِ حَتَّى مَا يَكُونُ بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَهَا إلَّا ذِرَاعٌ فَيَسْبِقُ عَلَيْهِ الْكِتَابُ فَيَعْمَلُ بِعَمَلِ أَهْلِ الْجَنَّةِ فَيَدْخُلُهَا".
source.translation: On the authority of Abdullah ibn Masood (ra), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he is the truthful, the believed, narrated to us, “Verily the creation of each one of you is brought together in his mother’s womb for forty days in the form of a nutfah (a drop), then he becomes an alaqah (clot of blood) for a like period, then a mudghah (morsel of flesh) for a like period, then there is sent to him the angel who blows his soul into him and who is commanded with four matters: to write down his rizq (sustenance), his life span, his actions, and whether he will be happy or unhappy (i.e., whether or not he will enter Paradise). By the One, other than Whom there is no deity, verily one of you performs the actions of the people of Paradise until there is but an arms length between him and it, and that which has been written overtakes him, and so he acts with the actions of the people of the Hellfire and thus enters it; and verily one of you performs the actions of the people of the Hellfire, until there is but an arms length between him and it, and that which has been written overtakes him and so he acts with the actions of the people of Paradise and thus he enters it.” [Bukhari & Muslim]

source.arabic: عَنْ أُمِّ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ أُمِّ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ عَائِشَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا، قَالَتْ: قَالَ: رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم "مَنْ أَحْدَثَ فِي أَمْرِنَا هَذَا مَا لَيْسَ مِنْهُ فَهُوَ رَدٌّ، وَفِي رِوَايَةٍ لِمُسْلِمٍ: مَنْ عَمِلَ عَمَلًا لَيْسَ عَلَيْهِ أَمْرُنَا فَهُوَ رَدٌّ".
source.translation: On the authority of the mother of the faithful, Aisha (ra), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, “He who innovates something in this matter of ours (i.e., Islam) that is not of it will have it rejected (by Allah).” [Bukhari & Muslim] In another version in Muslim it reads: “He who does an act which we have not commanded, will have it rejected (by Allah).”
source.citation: Source Citation: sunnah.com/nawawi40/5 (Hadith 5, Nawawi's Forty Hadith)

text: Understand the core framework of authenticity in religious practice. Learn how to describe boundaries, use precise passive expressions, and explain spiritual preservation in clear, modern English.
Narrated by Aisha (ra), the Mother of the Faithful. This lesson references established B1 level explanations from Sahih compilation commentaries to maintain precise terminology.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to perform these B1 linguistic tasks:
Identify the narrator, the core action (introducing unprescribed elements), and the outcome (rejection).
Define and correctly use five core Arabic-English equivalents related to guidance.
Understand and use grammar structures such as 'be + past participle' (is accepted / is rejected).
Formulate a objective summary of the text using references to sunnah.com and classical commentaries.

Language learners must separate different concepts of "new things". In standard B1 English, we classify developments into distinct areas. Differentiate these categories without assigning moral or legal rulings.
Creating brand-new medical treatments, communication tools, or high-speed transit systems.
Adjusting cultural dress styles or adoption of local dining etiquette and utensils.
Altering established forms of worship (e.g., adding an extra cycle to an obligatory prayer).
"A software developer designs a new mobile application to help people schedule their daily goals and checklists."

e.g., "Historical records were compiled on the authority of credible eyewitness accounts."
Introduces something new; here, an addition to religious practice.
e.g., "Scholars caution against anyone who innovates something foreign into classical principles."
The religion and practice of Islam referred to in the narration.
e.g., "Core ethical values in this matter of ours remain protected and unalterable."
Does not belong to it or form part of it.
e.g., "Any superstitious belief is not of it and must be discarded."
e.g., "Any ritual that contradicts authentic guidelines will be rejected."

source.arabic: عَنْ أَبِي عَبْدِ اللَّهِ النُّعْمَانِ بْنِ بَشِيرٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا، قَالَ: سَمِعْت رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم يَقُولُ: "إنَّ الْحَلَالَ بَيِّنٌ، وَإِنَّ الْحَرَامَ بَيِّنٌ، وَبَيْنَهُمَا أُمُورٌ مُشْتَبِهَاتٌ لَا يَعْلَمُهُنَّ كَثِيرٌ مِنْ النَّاسِ، فَمَنْ اتَّقَى الشُّبُهَاتِ فَقَد اسْتَبْرَأَ لِدِينِهِ وَعِرْضِهِ، وَمَنْ وَقَعَ فِي الشُّبُهَاتِ وَقَعَ فِي الْحَرَامِ، كَالرَّاعِي يَرْعَى حَوْلَ الْحِمَى يُوشِكُ أَنْ يَرْتَعَ فِيهِ، أَلَا وَإِنَّ لِكُلِّ مَلِكٍ حِمًى، أَلَا وَإِنَّ حِمَى اللَّهِ مَحَارِمُهُ، أَلَا وَإِنَّ فِي الْجَسَدِ مُضْغَةً إذَا صَلَحَتْ صَلَحَ الْجَسَدُ كُلُّهُ، وَإذَا فَسَدَتْ فَسَدَ الْجَسَدُ كُلُّهُ، أَلَا وَهِيَ الْقَلْبُ".
source.translation: On the authority of Abu `Abdullah al-Nu`man ibn Bashir (ra) who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "That which is lawful is clear and that which is unlawful is clear, and between the two of them are doubtful matters about which many people do not know. Thus he who avoids doubtful matters clears himself in regard to his religion and his honor, but he who falls into doubtful matters falls into that which is unlawful, like the shepherd who pastures around a sanctuary, almost pasturing therein. Truly every king has a sanctuary, and truly Allah's sanctuary is His prohibitions. Truly in the body there is a morsel of flesh which, if it be whole, all the body is whole, and which, if it be diseased, all of it is diseased. Truly it is the heart."
source.citation: Source: Sahih al-Bukhari & Sahih Muslim · sunnah.com/nawawi40/6

text: Learn how to distinguish between clear and unclear guidelines, express conditionality in decisions, and respond appropriately to uncertain or doubtful situations.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

source.translation: ‘On the authority of Tameem ibn Aus ad-Daree (ra): The Prophet (ﷺ) said, “The deen (religion) is naseehah (advice, sincerity).” We said, “To whom?” He (ﷺ) said, “To Allah, His Book, His Messenger, and to the leaders of the Muslims and their common folk.” [Muslim]’

text: Explore the deep meaning of naseehah (sincerity, advice) and learn how to offer guidance gently and privately in everyday settings.
Identify the core statement of Hadith 7 and its five direct recipients.

source.arabic: عَنْ ابْنِ عُمَرَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا، أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم قَالَ: "أُمِرْتُ أَنْ أُقَاتِلَ النَّاسَ حَتَّى يَشْهَدُوا أَنْ لَا إلَهَ إلَّا اللَّهُ وَأَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ، وَيُقِيمُوا الصَّلَاةَ، وَيُؤْتُوا الزَّكَاةَ؛ فَإِذَا فَعَلُوا ذَلِكَ عَصَمُوا مِنِّي دِمَاءَهُمْ وَأَمْوَالَهُمْ إلَّا بِحَقِّ الْإِسْلَامِ، وَحِسَابُهُمْ عَلَى اللَّهِ تَعَالَى".
source.translation: On the authority of Abdullah ibn Umar (ra): The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, “I have been ordered to fight against the people until they testify that there is none worthy of worship except Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and until they establish the salah and pay the zakat. And if they do that then they will have gained protection from me for their lives and property, unless [they commit acts that are punishable] in Islam, and their reckoning will be with Allah.” [Bukhari & Muslim]

source.arabic: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ عَبْدِ الرَّحْمَنِ بْنِ صَخْرٍ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: سَمِعْت رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم يَقُولُ: "مَا نَهَيْتُكُمْ عَنْهُ فَاجْتَنِبُوهُ، وَمَا أَمَرْتُكُمْ بِهِ فَأْتُوا مِنْهُ مَا اسْتَطَعْتُمْ، فَإِنَّمَا أَهْلَكَ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِكُمْ كَثْرَةُ مَسَائِلِهِمْ وَاخْتِلَافُهُمْ عَلَى أَنْبِيَائِهِمْ".
source.translation: "On the authority of Abu Hurayrah (ra): I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say, “What I have forbidden for you, avoid. What I have ordered you [to do], do as much of it as you can. For verily, it was only the excessive questioning and their disagreeing with their Prophets that destroyed [the nations] who were before you.” [Bukhari & Muslim]"

text: Identify two direct instructions from the Messenger (ﷺ).
Distinguish helpful clarification from excessive questioning.
State realistic personal ability & respect access needs.
Propose a compliant positive action plan for today.
Sincere clarification, disability/access accommodations, and safeguarding reports are always encouraged. Ask for help anytime.
Which question style aligns with the guidance of the Prophet (ﷺ)?
💡 Useful clarification ensures you can perform your duties within your limits. Excessive questioning breeds unnecessary rigidity and distress.
1. Total avoidance of harmful forbidden actions. 2. Commendable actions done to the best of your capacity.
Review these five core B1 expressions, observing how their meanings match the specific context of Hadith 9.
Not allowed; here, prohibited by religious guidance.
e.g., "Deceptive trade practices and fraudulent claims are strictly forbidden."
e.g., "Prudent managers actively avoid unnecessary risks that could jeopardize staff safety."
e.g., "Citizens are ordered to respect municipal regulations for environmental sanitation."
To the extent that you are able.
e.g., "Apply these safety procedures consistently as much as you can during peak hours."
Asking more questions than is useful or necessary.
e.g., "Excessive questioning about minor details often delays essential project milestones."
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
keep up with — continue at a manageable pace without falling behind.
cut back on — reduce the amount, frequency, or burden of an activity.
manageable pace — a sustainable speed that someone can maintain comfortably.
practical limit — a realistic boundary determined by available capacity and health.
can ≈ be able to; use be able to where can has no required verb form, for example will be able to
Not: We can to follow. | Use: We can follow (modal verbs take bare infinitive).
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.
Identify the action that best respects personal capability without falling into neglect.
What is one achievable good action you will commit to practice today?
Remember: Learners do not label actions "forbidden" or make general rules. We focus solely on our own positive ability today.
Explain to a peer how you stay consistent without getting overwhelmed. Keep it personal.
• State your action using "as much as I can"
• Share how asking for help is a sign of sincerity
• Avoid giving religious decrees or rulings
What primarily caused the destruction of nations before us, according to the Hadith?
Based on Nawawi Hadith 9. Supplementary guidance reviewed from IslamWeb. Qualified Islamic scholar review is recommended.

lessons.title: Choosing What Is Lawful and Good

source.arabic: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم "إنَّ اللَّهَ طَيِّبٌ لَا يَقْبَلُ إلَّا طَيِّبًا، وَإِنَّ اللَّهَ أَمَرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ بِمَا أَمَرَ بِهِ الْمُرْسَلِينَ فَقَالَ تَعَالَى: يَا أَيُّهَا الرُّسُلُ كُلُوا مِنْ الطَّيِّبَاتِ وَاعْمَلُوا صَالِحًا، وَقَالَ تَعَالَى: يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كُلُوا مِنْ طَيِّبَاتِ مَا رَزَقْنَاكُمْ ثُمَّ ذَكَرَ الرَّجُلَ يُطِيلُ السَّفَرَ أَشْعَثَ أَغْبَرَ يَمُدُّ يَدَيْهِ إلَى السَّمَاءِ: يَا رَبِّ! يَا رَبِّ! وَمَطْعَمُهُ حَرَامٌ، وَمَشْرَبُهُ حَرَامٌ، وَمَلْبَسُهُ حَرَامٌ، وَغُذِّيَ بِالْحَرَامِ، فَأَنَّى يُسْتَجَابُ لَهُ؟".
source.translation:
On the authority of Abu Hurayrah (ra): The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "Allah the Almighty is Pure and accepts only that which is pure. And verily Allah has commanded the Believers to do that which He has commanded the Messengers. So the Almighty has said:

'O (you) Messengers! Eat of the Tayyibat [all kinds of Halal (lawful) foods] and perform righteous deeds.' [23:51]

and the Almighty has said:

'O you who believe! Eat of the lawful things that We have provided you with' [2:172]

Then he (ﷺ) mentioned [the case of] a man who, having journeyed far, is disheveled and dusty, who spreads out his hands to the sky saying, "O Lord! O Lord!" while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, and he has been nourished unlawfully, so how can his supplication be answered?"

text: Choosing What Is Lawful and Good
Identify examples of pure and good provisions named in the texts.
Distinguish lawful-status questions from personal/cultural preferences.
Ask clear questions about product source and provenance.
Explain why honest, wholesome provision matters in personal supplication.
Remember: As students, we explore principles of lawful livelihood and honest work without issuing legal rulings (Fatwa) or judging individuals.
Read this modern scenario about food and product origin before we study the classical guidance.
Fariq purchases olive oil labeled organic and fair-trade. He wants to ensure the farmers were paid honestly and the product is pure.
Amina works diligently, completing her tasks on time without cutting corners. She believes her livelihood must be built on trust and truthfulness.
Why do you think knowing where our goods come from is valuable?
Review these five core B1 expressions, observing how their meanings match the specific context of Hadith 10.
Permitted; here, permitted under Islamic religious law.
e.g., "Earning a lawful income through fair service gives families true peace of mind."
Resources supplied to meet someone's needs.
e.g., "The farmer was deeply grateful for the abundant provision harvested after months of labor."
An action considered morally and religiously good.
e.g., "Volunteering to tutor disadvantaged students is a commendable righteous deed."
e.g., "The weary traveler had journeyed far across remote regions before finding shelter."
A prayer asking Allah for help, guidance, or forgiveness.
e.g., "In moments of genuine hardship, heartfelt supplication provides immense spiritual relief."
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
pick out — choose the purest or most suitable option from several possibilities.
turn down — refuse an unlawful, dubious, or unethical offer firmly.
wholesome choice — an ethical decision that promotes personal integrity and well-being.
good conduct — respectful, honest, and morally responsible behavior in daily dealings.
lawful ≈ permitted; good implies intrinsic moral purity and high quality
Not: This food is good for eat. | Use: This food is good to eat.
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.
Identify the core purpose: Why does the Hadith highlight honest and lawful livelihood?
When encountering complex financial or food-production questions, we ask a qualified scholar or professional rather than making personal assumptions.
Practice asking a trusted expert or supplier for clarification about a product's sourcing, without claiming legal judgment yourself.
"Does this shipment have certificates of origin?"
"Could you help me understand how this is sourced?"
All learning material corresponds directly to verified sources in Sunnah.com (Nawawi 40, Hadith 10). Learners are advised to seek expert guidance on complex matters of religious jurisprudence.

source.arabic: "دَعْ مَا يُرِيبُك إلَى مَا لَا يُرِيبُك"
source.translation: Leave that which makes you doubt for that which does not make you doubt.

text: Learn the foundational rule of leaving doubtful choices for pathways of assurance and peace of mind.
Paraphrase the principle of doubt and certainty.
Identify genuine uncertainty in daily scenarios.
Compare two options using logical criteria.
Construct questions to request reliable information.
Imagine you need to verify if an important community center is open today. You have two options:
"Someone said they might have changed hours, but nobody is totally sure."
"A direct announcement from the operators updated 5 minutes ago."
Which option leaves your heart more at peace?
Notice how Option A keeps your mind loops active, while Option B terminates doubt immediately with clear evidence.
“Leave that which makes you doubt for that which does not make you doubt.”
[At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasai]. At-Tirmidhi said that it was a good and sound (hasan saheeh) hadeeth.
Review these five core B1 expressions, observing how their meanings match the specific context of Hadith 11.
Uncertainty about whether something is true or right.
e.g., "If an investment causes moral doubt, it is far safer to decline the opportunity."
An option that is easy to understand or decide on.
e.g., "Choosing complete transparency in company accounts is always the clear choice."
To be confident that something is true or right.
e.g., "You will feel sure about your decision once all contract clauses are verified."
e.g., "Responsible journalists check first with reliable sources before printing breaking news."
e.g., "Taking the safer option protected the non-profit organization from severe legal liabilities."
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
clear up — resolve confusion, ambiguity, or misunderstandings through open dialogue.
work out — calculate or deduce a practical solution through deliberate analysis.
reliable information — verified facts that can be trusted without suspicion.
clear answer — a direct, unambiguous statement that leaves no room for confusion.
clarity ≠ certainty; clarity means being easy to understand, while certainty is conviction
Not: Explain me the issue. | Use: Explain the issue to me.
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.
Arrange these everyday situations on a line from highest doubt to highest certainty:
Eating food with no label from an unknown source.
Using an item where you heard mixed safety reviews.
Following a verified, officially stamped procedure.
To move from doubt to certainty, ask these three questions before deciding:

1. Is there a clear, verifiable document?
2. Can I ask a reliable, direct source?
3. What is the safer path if no proof is found?
Practice these phrases in class to express uncertainty gracefully and seek reliable alternatives.
Role: Take a pause to find reliable facts.
Partner A suggests taking a shortcut across a private yard without a path. Partner B uses “I am not sure” and proposes the “safer option” of staying on the main road.
I can paraphrase the principle of doubt and certainty.
I can identify genuine evidence-based uncertainty.
I can compare options with logical criteria.
I can request reliable information to gain clarity.

Do not reinforce obsessive doubt or compulsive checking (waswasa). Distinguish evidence-based uncertainty from recurring anxiety. Never let feelings alone produce religious rulings. Refer rulings and persistent distress to qualified support.

source.arabic: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم "مِنْ حُسْنِ إسْلَامِ الْمَرْءِ تَرْكُهُ مَا لَا يَعْنِيهِ".
source.translation: On the authority of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) said, “Part of the perfection of one’s Islam is his leaving that which does not concern him.”

text: Hadith 12 of Al-Nawawi's 40 Hadith collection, exploring healthy social focus and personal discipline.
Distinguish personal responsibility from unhelpful social intrusion.
Use respectful boundary language in English and classical concepts.
Identify active relevant duties in your own life sphere.
Offer appropriate help while respecting private boundaries.
Mastering my / your / their spheres of life, and expressing relevance using "has to do with."
In B1 Hadith study, we classify actions. Sort these modern scenarios into their correct moral category.
Offering clean food, or assisting an injured stranger
Completing tasks, fulfilling prayers, or household duties
Interrogating someone's finances or personal history
Abuse, danger, neglect, or suspicious conduct are never "private matters." Reporting these to a safe adult, counselor, or proper authority is always required and remains a primary duty.
A hasan (good) hadeeth which was related by at-Tirmidhi and others in this fashion.
Review these five core B1 expressions, observing how their meanings match the specific context of Hadith 12.
To affect someone or be relevant to them.
e.g., "Confidential employee salaries do not concern outside contractors."
A personal issue that is not public business.
e.g., "A family dispute is a private matter that neighbors should not gossip about."
To stop interfering with someone or something.
e.g., "Mature community members learn to leave alone issues that do not affect their responsibilities."
e.g., "Students must pay attention to their personal study habits rather than criticize others."
A duty to take care of something or act properly.
e.g., "Managing patient safety is the primary professional responsibility of every nurse."
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
leave out — exclude or omit non-essential or intrusive elements from a discussion.
deal with — take appropriate, decisive action to resolve an obligation or difficulty.
main concern — the primary priority or most pressing issue requiring undivided attention.
relevant detail — pertinent factual information directly connected to the matter at hand.
matter ≈ concern; an 'issue' often suggests an unresolved problem or controversy
Not: That concerns to me. | Use: That concerns me ('concern' is transitive).
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.
Your colleague is speaking very softly on a phone call. They seem distressed. What is the correct application of the Hadith?
Listen carefully to hear their secrets so you can tell others.
Respect their private matter, leave them alone, but offer general help later.
Correct! This honors boundaries while remaining supportive.
Interrogate them immediately because you have to know everything.
What if you witness physical harm or child neglect?
Answer: This is never "none of your business." Reporting danger is a heavy public duty in Islam.
In your speaking task, practice these 3 key B1 phrases to negotiate boundaries politely but firmly.
Usage: Politely ending curiosity about your own life.
Usage: Offering appropriate assistance without intrusive questions.
Usage: Stating your duty clearly to those who try to micromanage.
A: "Is everything alright with your finances?"
B: "Thank you for asking. That is private, but if you are free, this project is my responsibility."
This system utilizes authentic commentaries alongside IslamWeb guidelines. Note: reporting harm to authorities is always mandatory.

source.arabic: عَنْ أَبِي حَمْزَةَ أَنَسِ بْنِ مَالِكٍ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ خَادِمِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه و سلم قَالَ: "لَا يُؤْمِنُ أَحَدُكُمْ حَتَّى يُحِبَّ لِأَخِيهِ مَا يُحِبُّ لِنَفْسِهِ".
source.translation: None of you [truly] believes until he loves for his brother that which he loves for himself.

text: Discover the deep wisdom of wanting for your brother what you love for yourself, and learn how to put genuine goodwill into practice.
State the central comparison of the Hadith.
Learn to express genuine goodwill vocabulary in English.
Distinguish healthy competition from destructive envy.
Suggest supportive actions for peers and friends.
Consider this scenario: Your classmate or colleague achieves a major success (e.g., getting the highest mark or landing a dream role).
"Why did they get it instead of me? I worked just as hard. I hope their project fails so I can have another chance."
"I am so happy for you! I hope you succeed with your new responsibilities. Let me know how I can support you."
Which reaction nurtures a healthy, safe community? How does Reaction B benefit both people?
"None of you [truly] believes until he loves for his brother that which he loves for himself."
Review these five core B1 expressions, observing how their meanings match the specific context of Hadith 13.
To wish that someone achieves a good result.
e.g., "A supportive colleague will always hope you succeed in your career transitions."
Pleased about another person's good news.
e.g., "I am genuinely happy for you after hearing about your academic scholarship."
To give someone part of something or enjoy it together.
e.g., "Experienced researchers gladly share with you their findings to advance the whole field."
For two people or groups to succeed.
e.g., "In an ethical workplace, there is ample opportunity for both teams to do well."
e.g., "True friends will actively support you whenever you encounter unexpected difficulties."
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
look out for — watch vigilantly for opportunities to protect and support someone.
cheer on — encourage someone enthusiastically during an effort or milestone.
mutual support — reciprocal assistance that community members provide to one another.
kind wish — a friendly, benevolent expression of goodwill for another person's welfare.
want ≈ wish; hope indicates optimism for an achievable positive outcome
Not: I want that he succeeds. | Use: I want him to succeed (want takes object + infinitive).
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.
Example: "I want you to succeed" or "We hope them to do well."
Rewrite this jealous reaction into a supportive reaction using the target grammar:
Jealous: "I don't want him to get the high score."
I want him to do well and succeed...
Match the scenario with the supportive action:
Scenario: A peer opens a new bookstore.
Action: Buy a book or help share their opening.
Scenario: A classmate is struggling with English.
Action: Offer to share your notes and support them.
Practice expressing positive support aloud. Speak with a partner or Speak aloud .
Your classmate just started a new community project. Congratulate them, say you are happy for them, and offer practical assistance.
I am so happy for you that...
I hope you succeed with your new...
I want to share my... to support you.
Let's both do well in this...
I can state the central comparison of Hadith 13.
I can express goodwill using target vocabulary.
I understand how healthy competition differs from envy.
I can propose safe, supportive actions for others.
We'll prompt you to review these phrases in 3 days to build strong, long-term memory.
• Goodwill does not require reconciliation, affection, or contact with unsafe/harmful individuals.
• Personal boundaries remain valid. Wishing others well does not excuse past or present harm.
Developed in coordination with Islamic reviewers.

lessons.title: The Sanctity of Life and Due Process

source.arabic: عَنْ ابْنِ مَسْعُودٍ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم "لَا يَحِلُّ دَمُ امْرِئٍ مُسْلِمٍ [يشهد أن لا إله إلا الله، وأني رسول الله] إلَّا بِإِحْدَى ثَلَاثٍ: الثَّيِّبُ الزَّانِي، وَالنَّفْسُ بِالنَّفْسِ، وَالتَّارِكُ لِدِينِهِ الْمُفَارِقُ لِلْجَمَاعَةِ".
source.translation: “On the authority of Ibn Masood (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) said, “It is not permissible to spill the blood of a Muslim except in three [instances]: the married person who commits adultery, a life for a life, and the one who forsakes his religion and separates from the community.” [Al-Bukhari and Muslim]”

text: The Sanctity of Life and Due Process
Hadith 14 of Imam al-Nawawi. This module explores how classical legal texts establish the absolute protection of human life and prohibit private punishment.

High-risk content: study of classical capital guidelines. Strictly prohibited: private enforcement, reenactment, vigilantism, or application to any group. This is an educational analysis of judicial sovereignty and formal due process, not a complete legal code.
State that human life is absolutely protected as a default.
Identify classical text as formal, state-level legal content.
Completely reject private punishment and vigilantism.
Explain the necessity of central authority and due process.
Before studying the legal text, let us analyze how modern civic society maintains order and protects citizens from chaos.
If a driver runs a red light, can an ordinary citizen pull them over and write a ticket? Why or why not?
If a shopkeeper believes a customer stole an item, can they lock that customer in a back room permanently without calling the police?
Core Concept: Only formal courts and authorized officers have the legal mandate to process evidence and decide consequences.
What happens when individuals take the law into their own hands?
Society descends into insecurity and unchecked violence...
Review these five core B1 expressions, observing how their meanings match the specific context of Hadith 14.
A statement that human life should be kept safe from unlawful harm.
e.g., "International humanitarian conventions affirm that innocent life must be protected at all times."
A statement that individuals must not take unauthorized action.
e.g., "To prevent anarchy in civil disputes, no one may act alone without judicial sanction."
Information that helps show whether a claim is true.
e.g., "The prosecutor must present verifiable evidence beyond reasonable doubt before sentencing."
An official who hears cases and makes decisions in a court.
e.g., "The presiding judge examined both testimonies impartially before delivering the verdict."
Things that people are entitled to have or do.
e.g., "Fundamental civic rights ensure that every citizen receives fair legal representation."
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
stand up for — defend someone's legitimate rights courageously and fairly.
go through — experience and complete an official statutory process thoroughly.
due process — fair, transparent legal proceedings conducted in accordance with established rules.
personal safety — the condition of being protected from physical danger, injury, or threat.
sanctity ≈ sacredness; safety means practical protection from physical harm
Not: Everyone have rights. | Use: Everyone has rights ('everyone' takes a singular verb).
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.
Read each action below. Decide if it represents Formal Due Process or prohibited Private Revenge.
1. An individual tracks down a thief to physically reclaim stolen property by force.
2. An official court hears witnesses, reviews physical evidence, and issues a verdict.
3. A group of neighbors forms an unauthorized tribunal to punish a local vandal.
Why must judicial enforcement be exclusive to centralized, formal authority? Discuss the reasoning using these guidance blocks.
Explain how private parties are driven by personal emotion or bias, whereas formal courts must remain objective, examining evidence without personal stakes.
Prompt B: The Chaos of No Courts
Describe what a community looks like if anyone has the power to accuse, prosecute, and carry out punishment independently.
✓ Why individuals cannot punish others on their own.
✓ Use of the term "evidence" and "due process".
I can state that life is absolutely protected by default.
I can identify that legal parameters belong to official state courts.
I understand that all private vigilante punishment is prohibited.
I can explain how due process prevents chaos in society.
Review complete. You can retry any step or return to the Curriculum Map.

source.arabic: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم قَالَ: "مَنْ كَانَ يُؤْمِنُ بِاَللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ فَلْيَقُلْ خَيْرًا أَوْ لِيَصْمُتْ، وَمَنْ كَانَ يُؤْمِنُ بِاَللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ فَلْيُكْرِمْ جَارَهُ، وَمَنْ كَانَ يُؤْمِنُ بِاَللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ فَلْيُكْرِمْ ضَيْفَهُ".
source.translation: “On the authority of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) said: Let him who believes in Allah and the Last Day speak good, or keep silent; and let him who believes in Allah and the Last Day be generous to his neighbour; and let him who believes in Allah and the Last Day be generous to his guest.”

text: Hadith 15 of Imam al-Nawawi. Learn to express care through positive speech and hospitality. This module explores how constructive language builds supportive social units.

• Silence Mandate: Recommended silence must never suppress reporting harm, testimony, corrective feedback, or seeking help.
• Hospitality Limits: Welcoming guests must not compromise privacy, resources, personal safety, or consent.
• Standard: Requires Islamic scholar and safeguarding review.
Name three specific pro-social behaviours taught in the Hadith.
Evaluate helpful versus harmful speech in modern public channels.
Make a polite offer to a guest using correct modal grammar.
Demonstrate culturally respectful welcoming language to neighbours.
Examine the digital comments below. Identify the harmful language, then compare which expressions make guests feel truly safe and welcome.
"If you don't agree with my review, just leave. Nobody wants your opinion here anyway."
→ Edit Suggestion: Keep silent instead of expressing needless frustration.
"Thank you for sharing your thoughts. Please let us know if there is anything we can do to make your stay more comfortable."
→ Benefit: Establishes immediate psychological safety and hospitality.
Core Concept: Hospitality is a proactive civic virtue. It requires active generosity in speech, environment, and physical care.
Why is silence often better than defensive speech?
Review these five core B1 expressions, observing how their meanings match the specific context of Hadith 15.
To say something truthful, helpful, or kind.
e.g., "Diplomats strive to speak well in tense negotiations to foster understanding."
e.g., "When you lack verified information about a controversy, it is wisest to keep silent."
A person who lives near you.
e.g., "An attentive resident checks on an elderly neighbour during severe winter storms."
To receive a visitor warmly and respectfully.
e.g., "Traditional households take special pride in how warmly they welcome a guest."
e.g., "Philanthropists choose to be generous with both financial donations and personal time."
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
get along with — maintain a friendly, cooperative relationship with others.
invite in — welcome someone courteously into your home, workplace, or gathering.
kind words — gentle, comforting language that brings reassurance and encouragement.
warm welcome — an enthusiastic and friendly greeting given to a visitor.
welcome ≈ greet warmly; host means to receive and look after guests officially
Not: She said me hello. | Use: She said hello to me.
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.
Read the following situations and select the action that best represents appropriate speech or generous help:
You see an online post containing inaccurate but harmless personal opinions about cooking.
Your elderly neighbour is struggling to carry heavy groceries up the shared stairs.
A guest arrives at your house after a long journey in cold weather.
Role-play a hospitality scenario. Practice expressing generosity while maintaining necessary personal and household safety boundaries.
"Would you like to step inside the lobby where it is warm while I fetch your parcel?"
"I would love to help, but I cannot invite visitors inside at this late hour. Let me help you out here instead."
✓ Use of "would you like" or "may I" for polite offers.
✓ Balanced generosity and household safety awareness.
✓ Clear distinction between helpful speech and silence.
Need another try? Reset progress to review vocabulary or practice scenarios.

source.arabic: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ أَنَّ رَجُلًا قَالَ لِلنَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه و سلم أَوْصِنِي. قَالَ: لَا تَغْضَبْ، فَرَدَّدَ مِرَارًا، قَالَ: لَا تَغْضَبْ.
source.translation: “On the authority of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that a man said to the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him), “Counsel me,” so he said, “Do not become angry.” The man repeated his request several times, and each time he said, “Do not become angry.” [Al-Bukhari]”

text: Hadith 16 of Imam al-Nawawi. Learn how to recognize anger as a natural emotion while choosing constructive behavior and establishing safe boundaries.

Anger is a normal human emotion and must never be shamed. However, victims of harm are never expected to tolerate abuse. Threats, violence, or loss of safety require immediate adult support or emergency safeguarding. No forced personal disclosure is required.
Distinguish natural emotions from chosen behaviors
Use practical phrases to request a safe pause
Choose safe, non-harmful responses to provocation
Our bodies often experience neutral physical warning signs when tension rises. Recognizing these signals helps us request a pause before reacting.
You notice your breathing getting faster, your hands tensing, or your face feeling warm. These are natural physiological responses.
A pause creates space between the initial spark of emotion and your final chosen response. It prevents sudden escalation.
Core Concept: Feeling anger is a natural experience. Behavior is what we consciously regulate and choose.
What is one personal signal that tells you to take a pause?
Review these five core B1 expressions, observing how their meanings match the specific context of Hadith 16.
e.g., "It is normal to feel angry when treated unfairly, but one must control how one acts."
To require a short break before continuing.
e.g., "During intense disputes, professional negotiators often need a pause to regain composure."
To have a conversation at another time.
e.g., "When emotions are running high, it is much safer to agree to talk later."
To become less upset or angry.
e.g., "Deep breathing exercises help emergency workers calm down under extreme pressure."
To avoid causing pain or harm to others.
e.g., "Responsible adults resolve conflicts with patience so they do not hurt anyone."
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
calm down — become progressively less agitated, tense, or upset.
walk away — leave an escalating conflict deliberately before damage occurs.
measured response — a carefully calculated, calm reply delivered with emotional control.
tense moment — a brief interval of acute stress, anxiety, or interpersonal friction.
calm ≠ silent; calm denotes composed inner control, not mere absence of speech
Not: He became anger. | Use: He became angry ('become' takes an adjective).
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.
Read each scenario. Choose the action that separates the natural feeling from escalating actions.
You notice your heart rate rises rapidly. What is the wisest response?
You feel angry about a score. How can you act calmly?
Recognize the signal and step outside.
Use the safety script template below to practice communicating boundaries clearly with a family member or friend.
"I feel angry because [reason]. I need a pause right now. Let us talk later."
"I feel angry because my space wasn't respected. I need a pause. Let us talk later when we are both calm."
✓ Focus on your immediate feeling without blaming.
✓ State the need for a pause explicitly.
✓ Establish a future time to revisit the talk.
Recognized that anger is natural but choices are controlled
Identified physiological warning signs of anger
Practiced requesting a safe pause before escalation
Remaining attempts for this unit: 2 of 3

source.arabic: عَنْ أَبِي يَعْلَى شَدَّادِ بْنِ أَوْسٍ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ عَنْ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم قَالَ: "إنَّ اللَّهَ كَتَبَ الْإِحْسَانَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ، فَإِذَا قَتَلْتُمْ فَأَحْسِنُوا الْقِتْلَةَ، وَإِذَا ذَبَحْتُمْ فَأَحْسِنُوا الذِّبْحَةَ، وَلْيُحِدَّ أَحَدُكُمْ شَفْرَتَهُ، وَلْيُرِحْ ذَبِيحَتَهُ".
source.translation: “Shaddad ibn Aws reported: Verily Allah has prescribed ihsan (proficiency, perfection) in all things. So if you kill then kill well; and if you slaughter, then slaughter well. Let each one of you sharpen his blade and let him spare suffering to the animal he slaughters.”

text: Hadith 17 of Imam al-Nawawi. This lesson centers on the comprehensive concept of Ihsan—approaching every action, life, and living being with the utmost skill, empathy, and care.

This unit teaches general compassion, prompt preparation, and ethical animal treatment. Graphic illustrations, physical enactment, or instruction on ritual/procedural slaughter laws are strictly out of scope.
Define the linguistic and ethical scope of Ihsan in daily tasks.
Identify correct and humane preparations to prevent harm.
Explain the priority of sparing suffering over convenience.
Apply pre-task tool calibration to a neutral educational task.
Doing a job with care begins long before the task starts. Look at these non-graphic preparation examples.
A gardener tills, moisturizes, and clears debris before planting fragile seeds, preventing root shock and stress.
An architect shaves the charcoal tip beforehand. Blunt tools tear paper and destroy clean designs, causing avoidable waste.
Core Connection: In prophetic ethics, the condition and preparation of tools is a metric of mercy and competence.
How does careful preparation beforehand show mercy to those affected by our work?
Review these five core B1 expressions, observing how their meanings match the specific context of Hadith 17.
To touch or manage something carefully.
e.g., "Veterinarians always handle injured animals with care to minimize stress."
To make pain or distress less severe.
e.g., "Palliative care specialists work tirelessly to reduce suffering for terminally ill patients."
The equipment suitable for a particular task.
e.g., "Using the right tool ensures surgical procedures are swift, clean, and safe."
To get ready ahead of an activity.
e.g., "Surgeons prepare before an operation to prevent unnecessary complications."
To behave gently and considerately towards someone.
e.g., "Ethical guidelines instruct researchers to treat all laboratory animals kindly."
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
look after — provide continuous, attentive care for someone or something in need.
reach out — offer compassionate help or practical support to those experiencing hardship.
gentle manner — a mild, considerate disposition that sets others at ease.
high standard — an exemplary benchmark of professional and ethical excellence.
mercy ≈ compassion; kindness is everyday practical benevolence
Not: Treat them with merciful. | Use: Treat them with mercy (prepositions take nouns).
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.
Sequence the following steps to ensure Ihsan is upheld. Tap to drag and reorder. Focus on zero-distress logic:
Gently guide the animal to a comfortable area, away from noise, ensuring no sudden or terrifying movements.
Calibrate and sharpen tools in secret
Sharpening blades must be done entirely out of the animal's sight or smell range to avoid psychological trauma.
Use the single fastest mechanism to ensure instant relief, avoiding any slow procedural delays.
How does prophetic preparation directly prevent trauma? Discuss this principle using these non-graphic prompts.
"Slaughtering an animal in front of another is strictly prohibited." Discuss how visual boundaries protect animal emotional welfare.
"Sharpen the blade thoroughly." Compare how dull tools create prolonged tearing, whereas perfected tools end sensation instantly.
✓ At least one example of imperative purpose (e.g., "Use... to...").
✓ Accurate usage of the term "Ihsan" and "prevent avoidable suffering".
• Empathy in action: Compassion across all life. • Ethical tool design & hidden prep procedures. • Imperative and purpose grammar check.

source.arabic: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ جُنْدَبِ بْنِ جُنَادَةَ، وَأَبِي عَبْدِ الرَّحْمَنِ مُعَاذِ بْنِ جَبَلٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا، عَنْ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم قَالَ: "اتَّقِ اللَّهَ حَيْثُمَا كُنْت، وَأَتْبِعْ السَّيِّئَةَ الْحَسَنَةَ تَمْحُهَا، وَخَالِقْ النَّاسَ بِخُلُقٍ حَسَنٍ".
source.translation: On the authority of Abu Dharr Jundub ibn Junadah and Abu Abdur-Rahman Muadh bin Jabal (ra), from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Have taqwa (fear) of Allah wherever you may be, and follow up a bad deed with a good deed which will wipe it out, and behave well towards the people."

text: Learn how to constructively address and correct accidental mistakes, express genuine remorse, and take meaningful actions to restore balance in relationships and daily actions.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Acknowledge the core prophetic guidance on self-awareness, pursuing corrective good deeds, and maintaining outstanding character.
Express accountability for structured, low-stakes scenarios without feeling pressured to share personal or private struggles.
Recognize when restoring balance requires a mix of apologies, safe physical rectifications, or seeking experienced counseling.
Synthesize the Past Simple to state an accidental mistake with the Future Simple to initiate positive repair ('I did... so I will...').
What do we do when things go wrong?
"You accidentally spill a cup of coffee on your coworker's clean desk notes. You feel bad."
Which reaction best helps fix the relationship?
• Ignore it and hope they do not notice.
✓ Apologize immediately, help dry the papers, and offer to reprint them.
• Get angry at the cup for being placed poorly.
Unlock the full prophetic narration by thinking through how we mend interpersonal slip-ups first.
Being conscious of God's presence and our actions wherever we are.
Actively performing a virtuous act immediately after an error.
Interacting with others with beautiful, kind, and fair manners.
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
make up for — do good after causing a problem.
put right — correct a mistake or problem.
positive action — a helpful step toward improvement.
honest apology — a sincere statement accepting a mistake.
mistake ≈ error; fault can also mean responsibility
Not: I did a mistake. | Use: I made a mistake.
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.
Review these five core B1 expressions, observing how their meanings match the specific context of Hadith 18.
Did something incorrectly or made an error.
e.g., "The junior accountant realized she had made a mistake on the quarterly report."
e.g., "He was sincerely sorry for the misunderstanding caused by his abrupt email."
To correct a mistake or repair a problem.
e.g., "Whenever you make an error, take immediate responsibility and put it right."
A question asking which helpful action is possible.
e.g., "After addressing the grievance, ask yourself: what good can I do to rebuild team morale?"
To behave towards others with kindness and respect.
e.g., "The golden rule of community leadership is to treat people well under all circumstances."
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
make up for — do good after causing a problem.
put right — restore a situation to good order.
positive action — constructive effort taken to improve a situation.
honest apology — a sincere expression of regret for a mistake.
repair ≈ fix; restore means return to an original condition
Not: I will make up it. | Use: I will make up for it.
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.
"Ali accidentally deleted his team's shared project outline. He needs to acknowledge the error and choose a proportionate, safe repair."
• He keeps silent and hopes they ask the tech team instead.
I made a mistake. I will put it right.
• He blames the software design for being confusing.
Forgot to call a friend back:
Send a friendly text and catch up later.
Apologize and buy an identical replacement.
Briefly apologize and quietly join the agenda.
Repairing mistakes is about restoring fairness and hope. A good deed towards someone else does not erase their right to restitution or safety.
Practice explaining an accidental mistake and its prospective repair. Speak aloud or write your answer using the B1 patterns.
Scenario A: Spilling tea on a table cloth
Formula: I spilled... so I will wash...
Scenario B: Borrowing a book and folding a page
Formula: I folded... so I will buy...
Scenario C: Forgetting a clean spoon for dessert
Formula: I forgot... so I will fetch...
Mindfulness (Taqwa), pursuing errors with subsequent good deeds, and outstanding character.
Differentiating between harmless, minor slip-ups and those requiring restitution or structural support.
Selecting restorative actions (apologies, safe direct repair, or counseling) depending on the situation.
Synthesize Key B1 Vocabulary and Grammar
Constructing simple 'I did... so I will...' structures to clarify remorse and propose future goodwill.

This lesson highlights the constructive, hopeful path of prophetic guidance: recognizing minor errors and correcting them with active, sincere good deeds. It maintains personal boundaries and highlights outstanding social conduct.
No public confessions forced on learners
One good deed does not erase other people's rights
Repair may require real restitution or expert counsel
Hope over humiliation is the core pedagogical driver

source.arabic: عَنْ أَبِي الْعَبَّاسِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَبَّاسٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: كُنْت خَلْفَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَوْمًا، فَقَالَ: "يَا غُلَامُ! إنِّي أُعَلِّمُك كَلِمَاتٍ: احْفَظْ اللَّهَ يَحْفَظْك، احْفَظْ اللَّهَ تَجِدْهُ تُجَاهَك، إذَا سَأَلْت فَاسْأَلْ اللَّهَ، وَإِذَا اسْتَعَنْت فَاسْتَعِنْ بِاللَّهِ، وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ الْأُمَّةَ لَوْ اجْتَمَعَتْ عَلَى أَنْ يَنْفَعُوك بِشَيْءٍ لَمْ يَنْفَعُوك إلَّا بِشَيْءٍ قَدْ كَتَبَهُ اللَّه لَك، وَلَوْ اجْتَمَعُوا عَلَى أَنْ يَضُرُّوك بِشَيْءٍ لَمْ يَضُرُّوك إلَّا بِشَيْءٍ قَدْ كَتَبَهُ اللَّه عَلَيْك؛ رُفِعَتْ الْأَقْلَامُ، وَجَفَّتْ الصُّحُفُ".
source.translation: On the authority of Abu al-Abbas Abdullah bin Abbas (ra) who said: One day I was behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and he said: "O young man, I shall teach you some words: Be mindful of Allah and Allah will protect you. Be mindful of Allah and you will find Him in front of you. If you ask, ask of Allah; if you seek help, seek help of Allah. Know that if the nation were to gather together to benefit you with anything, they would not benefit you except with what Allah had already prescribed for you, and if they were to gather together to harm you with anything, they would not harm you except with what Allah had already prescribed against you. The pens have been lifted and the pages have dried."

text: Distinguish active, responsible trust in Allah from passive fatalism. Practice expressing reliance and taking steps within your personal control in English.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Recall advice to the young narrator, Ibn Abbas (ra).
Distinguish active trust (Tawakkul) from passive fatalism.
Identify a responsible, healthy action in any test.
Express reliance clearly without claiming complete outcomes.
Look at these neutral situations. Which ones can you directly control?
Your study efforts before an English test
Choosing to eat a healthy meal
Warm-up completed. Next: Read & Listen to the exact Hadith narration.
"Be mindful of Allah, and you will find Him in front of you." Trusting Allah begins with understanding what lies in our hands to act upon, and what rests solely in Divine Decree.
Notice how "if" clauses are used to establish conditions ("if you ask, ask of Allah").
Review these five core B1 expressions, observing how their meanings match the specific context of Hadith 19.
To rely on Allah while taking appropriate practical steps.
e.g., "While taking all practical precautions, wise believers ultimately trust Allah with the final result."
e.g., "Never hesitate to ask for help when a professional assignment exceeds your current expertise."
To make the effort that is within my ability.
e.g., "I will study diligently every evening and do what I can to prepare for the board examination."
Outside what I can determine or change.
e.g., "Market fluctuations are beyond my control, so I concentrate strictly on financial discipline."
To do the next action needed to move forward.
e.g., "Once you have consulted your mentors, take the next step with firm determination."
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
turn to — seek help, reassurance, or guidance from someone trusted.
carry on — persevere forward steadily despite emotional uncertainty.
firm trust — deep, unshakable confidence in a person, plan, or divine wisdom.
next step — the immediate constructive action required in a process.
trust ≈ rely on; hope is wishing for a good result, while trust is active reliance
Not: I trust on Allah. | Use: I trust in Allah (or trust Allah).
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.
Map a healthy exam prep scenario. Sort these items correctly:
Be mindful of Allah, and He will protect you.
If you ask, ask of Allah; if you seek help, seek help of Allah.
Know that victory comes with patience and relief with affliction.
Construct a spoken answer explaining how you prepare for a challenging task, combining one personal active plan with one expression of reliance.
"I will do what I can by preparing my tools, and then I will trust Allah with the final outcome."

The linguistic concepts in this lesson are structured strictly for language acquisition. All theological definitions are supplementary. Seeking professional/medical support and safeguarding help is an essential duty and does not contradict Tawakkul.
Can recall Advice to narrator (Ibn Abbas)
Successfully identified: "O young man, I shall teach you some words: Be mindful of..."
Mapped active preparation under "Within Control" and rejected passive fatalism.
This lesson covers the primary Nawawi Forty narration of Jami` at-Tirmidhi and notes secondary additions clearly.

source.arabic: عَنْ أَبِي مَسْعُودٍ عُقْبَةَ بْنِ عَمْرٍو الْأَنْصَارِيِّ الْبَدْرِيِّ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم "إنَّ مِمَّا أَدْرَكَ النَّاسُ مِنْ كَلَامِ النُّبُوَّةِ الْأُولَى: إذَا لَمْ تَسْتَحِ فَاصْنَعْ مَا شِئْت"
source.translation: On the authority of Abu Masood Uqbah bin ’Amr al-Ansaree al-Badree (ra), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Verily, from what was learnt by the people from the speech of the earliest prophecy is: If you feel no shame, then do as you wish." [Al-Bukhari]
source.citation: Source: Sahih al-Bukhari · Hadith 20, Nawawi's Forty Hadith · sunnah.com/nawawi40/20

text: Understand modesty (haya) as an inner compass for healthy self-reflection and protective boundaries, rather than absolute permission to make harmful choices.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain modesty as a moral guide rather than permission to harm.
Distinguish healthy modesty (haya) from unhealthy toxic shame.
Evaluate safe moral decisions in fictional scenarios.
State a respectful, healthy personal boundary clearly in English.

• When nobody is watching, how do you make choices?
• What quiet feeling tells you a choice is wrong before you actually do it?
This private awareness is the essence of Haya (modesty) — a protective moral shield, not a source of fear or self-punishment.
You are activating your moral awareness. Complete this warm-up to unlock the exact prophetic teaching.
Haya is voluntary and honors personal dignity. Unlike coercive pressure, it respects healthy private boundaries and protects individual safety.

This is not an invitation to act freely without boundaries. Rather, it is a conditional warnings statement: If a person lacks any healthy internal shield, there is nothing left to guide their actions.
Modesty (Haya) here is defined as moral self-regulation: holding oneself back from harmful actions because of personal integrity and respect for others.
Review these five core B1 expressions, observing how their meanings match the specific context of Hadith 20.
An action considered correct or morally good.
e.g., "Whistleblowers often face workplace hostility simply for doing the right thing."
In a way that others can see or hear; without secrecy.
e.g., "Ethical leaders discuss organizational challenges openly to invite constructive solutions."
Freedom from unwanted access to personal information or affairs.
e.g., "Medical ethics strictly guarantee patient privacy during all consultations."
Might cause injury, pain, or damage to another person.
e.g., "Do not spread unverified rumors because reckless words may harm someone unfairly."
An alternative that is more suitable or beneficial.
e.g., "Choosing respectful dialogue over confrontation is invariably the better choice."
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
hold back — exercise self-restraint and stop oneself from acting inappropriately.
tone down — moderate one's language or behavior to prevent friction.
personal boundary — a clear limit established to protect psychological comfort and privacy.
quiet confidence — serene inner assurance that does not need boastful display.
modest ≠ shy; modest describes not boasting, while shy describes feeling reserved or uncomfortable with others
Not: She is a modesty person. | Use: She is a modest person (use adjective before noun).
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.

• Voluntary self-regulation based on personal dignity.
• Protects self and others from harm.
• Respects safety and healthy physical/personal boundaries.

• Coercive pressure from outer forces.
• Makes the person feel broken, worthless, or victimized.
• Leads to harmful secrecy and concealment of abuse.
Modesty should never be used as a coercive purity message or to justify body shaming. True haya honors personal choice.

Use the fictional example only. Do not share personal experiences.

Scenario: Tariq’s classmates ask him to post a video of another student without permission.

1. Choose the action that protects the student’s privacy.
2. Explain your choice to a partner.
3. Use this frame: “If Tariq values privacy, he will not…”
Practice expressing clear boundaries safely in English. Modesty never means remaining silent about safety or abuse.
Learners can explain why 'do as you wish' acts as a solemn warnings statement about lacking a moral compass, rather than an active endorsement to harm.
Learners successfully contrast voluntary, dignity-affirming haya against coercive external humiliation (toxic shame).
Learners apply first-conditional language constructs to safely evaluate fictional ethical challenges regarding group pressure and personal privacy.
Learners formulate and practice clear, polite statements of personal boundaries to defend individual dignity and reject boundary violations.
Hadith 20 provides B1 learners with a powerful platform to express conditional ethical commit-ments while practicing English.
Practice target vocabulary including 'privacy', 'may harm', and grammar structures using first conditional rules in future lessons.

source.arabic: عَنْ أَبِي عَمْرٍو وَقِيلَ: أَبِي عَمْرَةَ سُفْيَانَ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: "قُلْت: يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ! قُلْ لِي فِي الْإِسْلَامِ قَوْلًا لَا أَسْأَلُ عَنْهُ أَحَدًا غَيْرَك؛ قَالَ: قُلْ: آمَنْت بِاَللَّهِ ثُمَّ اسْتَقِمْ".
source.translation: On the authority of Abu Amr — and he is also called Abu Amrah — Sufyan bin Abdullah ath-Thaqafee… I said, “O Messenger of Allah, tell me something about al-Islam which I can ask of no one but you.” He said, “Say I believe in Allah — and then be steadfast .” [Muslim]

text: Understand the connection between a simple statement of faith and continuous, steady actions. Practice explaining personal motivation and routines using sequenced English structures.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Identify a spiritual question and its concise, practical answer in Hadith 21.
Explain five core expressions: 'believe in', 'remain steadfast', 'keep going', 'consistent action', and 'ask for guidance'.
Use the first...then grammar structure to sequence belief statements and action plans.
Describe one safe, consistent positive action or habit in clear English.
Steadfastness begins with daily consistency. Think about your neutral, everyday routines—like watering a plant, studying English daily, or keeping a clean workspace.
Is it easier to make a big promise once, or to do a tiny positive action every single day without stopping? Why?
Unlock the exact Hadith text by reflecting on consistency first.
In this lesson, we look at how belief (iman) becomes a guiding light that shapes steady, beautiful habits.
Listen to correct pronunciation and repeat after the teacher to perfect your B1 conversational rhythm.
Observe the transition word "then" (ثُمَّ) in the Hadith. It connects the statement of faith directly to the continuous, lifelong journey of steadfastness.
Review these five core B1 expressions, observing how their meanings match the specific context of Hadith 21.
To have faith or trust in someone or something.
e.g., "To build a meaningful career, you must believe in your core values and ethical standards."
To stay committed and consistent despite difficulty.
e.g., "True champions remain steadfast through rigorous training schedules and temporary setbacks."
e.g., "Even when immediate results are not visible, keep going with your daily vocabulary study."
A deed or practice repeated reliably over time.
e.g., "Consistent action every morning produces long-term language fluency."
e.g., "When navigating complex regulatory requirements, ask for guidance from senior counsel."
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
hold on — maintain firm resolve and grip during periods of acute trial.
keep going — proceed continuously along a path without stopping.
steady commitment — an enduring, dependable dedication to a noble goal over time.
long-term goal — a meaningful objective that requires sustained effort across months or years.
steadfast ≈ firm; stubborn means unreasonable refusal to change in the face of reason
Not: Remain to be patient. | Use: Remain patient ('remain' takes an adjective).
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.
Practice sequencing a belief statement with a realistic, consistent action plan using our core grammar structure.
First, I believe. Then, I act consistently.
"First, I ask for guidance, then I remain steadfast on my learning schedule."
Match the B1 vocabulary term to its correct action plan.
[ ask for guidance ]  →  "Seek direction from the teacher."
Describe one safe, consistent habit in your life that helps you build focus or knowledge. Use the target vocabulary and grammar structure.
"First, I choose my daily focus. Then, I keep going on my schedule so I can remain steadfast."
My example is a safe, positive habit.

The concept of remaining steadfast (istiqamah) requires qualified theological explanation. It must be clearly taught as a positive, balanced spiritual principle that never justifies harmful rigidity, ignoring changed evidence, or refusing legitimate help.
Can you clearly identify the question Sufyan bin Abdullah asked, and the short answer given by the Prophet (ﷺ)?
Describe how you connect your daily actions to your beliefs using 'first' and 'then'.
Hadith 21 teaches that complete sincerity is paired with steadfast habits. You have successfully finished all B1 language exercises!

source.arabic: عَنْ أَبِي عَبْدِ اللَّهِ جَابِرِ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ الْأَنْصَارِيِّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا: "أَنَّ رَجُلًا سَأَلَ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه و سلم فَقَالَ: أَرَأَيْت إذَا صَلَّيْت الْمَكْتُوبَاتِ، وَصُمْت رَمَضَانَ، وَأَحْلَلْت الْحَلَالَ، وَحَرَّمْت الْحَرَامَ، وَلَمْ أَزِدْ عَلَى ذَلِكَ شَيْئًا؛ أَأَدْخُلُ الْجَنَّةَ؟ قَالَ: نَعَمْ".
source.translation: On the authority of Abu Abdullah Jabir bin Abdullah al-Ansaree (ra) that a man questioned the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saying: "Do you think that if I perform the obligatory prayers, fast in Ramadhan, treat as lawful that which is halal, and treat as forbidden that which is haram, and do not increase upon that in voluntary good deeds, then I shall enter Paradise?" He replied, "Yes."

source.arabic: عَنْ أَبِي مَالِكٍ الْحَارِثِ بْنِ عَاصِمٍ الْأَشْعَرِيِّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: "الطَّهُورُ شَطْرُ الْإِيمَانِ، وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ تَمْلأُ الْمِيزَانَ، وَسُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ تَمْلأَنِ -أَوْ تَمْلأُ- مَا بَيْنَ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ، وَالصَّلَاةُ نُورٌ، وَالصَّدَقَةُ بُرْهَانٌ، وَالصَّبْرُ ضِيَاءٌ، وَالْقُرْآنُ حُجَّةٌ لَك أَوْ عَلَيْك، كُلُّ النَّاسِ يَغْدُو، فَبَائِعٌ نَفْسَهُ فَمُعْتِقُهَا أَوْ مُوبِقُهَا". (رواه مسلم)
source.translation: “Purity is half of iman (faith). ‘Al-hamdu lillah’ (all praise and gratitude belong to Allah) fills the scales, and ‘subhan Allah’ (free from imperfection is Allah) and ‘Al-hamdu lillah’ fill that which is between heaven and earth. Prayer is a light, charity is a proof, patience is illumination, and the Qur’an is a proof either for you or against you. Every person starts his day as a vendor of his soul, either freeing it or bringing about its ruin.”

text: Hadith 23 of Imam al-Nawawi. This module explores how the purification of self, internalizing praise, and steady patience light up the believer's path and dictate their daily moral trade.

Scales, light, proof, and selling one's soul are figurative and theological expressions. This curriculum requires qualified Islamic Islamic Scholar review; strictly avoid fear-based pressure or literalist oversimplification.
Identify the sequence of metaphors and daily choices.
Before diving into the sacred text, reflect on how we naturally use "light", "proof", and "patience" as guiding elements in our daily modern decisions.
We say clarity is "seeing the light" because it guides us out of confusion. What clarifies your path?
We demand proof to back up claims. In our morals, actions act as the ultimate proof of our sincerity.
Everyday Choice: We negotiate our time, values, and focus every single morning. We are constantly trading our effort for transient or lasting rewards.
How do you choose to "sell" your daily energy?
By investing in patience and clarity rather than instant comfort.

source.arabic: عن أبي ذر الغفاري رضي الله عنه عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فيما يرويه عن ربه تبارك وتعالى أنه قال: «يا عبادي، إني حرمت الظلم على نفسي، وجعلته بينكم محرما، فلا تظالموا. يا عبادي، كلكم ضال إلا من هديته، فاستهدوني أهدكم. يا عبادي، كلكم جائع إلا من أطعمته، فاستطعموني أطعمكم. يا عبادي، كلكم عار إلا من كسوته، فاستكسوني أكسكم. يا عبادي، إنكم تخطئون بالليل والنهار، وأنا أغفر الذنوب جميعا، فاستغفروني أغفر لكم. يا عبادي، إنكم لن تبلغوا ضري فتضروني، ولن تبلغوا نفعي فتنفعوني. يا عبادي، لو أن أولكم وآخركم وإنسكم وجنكم كانوا على أتقى قلب رجل واحد منكم، ما زاد ذلك في ملكي شيئا. يا عبادي، لو أن أولكم وآخركم وإنسكم وجنكم كانوا على أفجر قلب رجل واحد منكم، ما نقص ذلك من ملكي شيئا. يا عبادي، لو أن أولكم وآخركم وإنسكم وجنكم قاموا في صعيد واحد، فسألوني، فأعطيت كل واحد مسألته، ما نقص ذلك مما عندي إلا كما ينقص المخيط إذا أدخل البحر. يا عبادي، إنما هي أعمالكم أحصيها لكم، ثم أوفيكم إياها، فمن وجد خيرا فليحمد الله، ومن وجد غير ذلك فلا يلومن إلا نفسه». رواه مسلم.
source.translation:
Abu Dharr reported that the Prophet related these words from his Lord:
“My servants, I have prohibited oppression for Myself and have prohibited it among you; therefore, do not oppress each other.
My servants, you are all without guidance except those I guide. Ask Me for guidance, and I will guide you.
My servants, you are all hungry except those I feed. Ask Me for food, and I will feed you.
My servants, you are all without clothing except those I clothe. Ask Me for clothing, and I will clothe you.
My servants, you sin during the night and day, and I forgive every sin. Ask Me for forgiveness, and I will forgive you.
My servants, you cannot reach Me with harm or benefit.
My servants, if all of you, from the first to the last, humans and jinn, had the most devout heart, that would add nothing to My dominion. If all of you had the most wicked heart, that would take nothing from My dominion.
My servants, if all of you stood together and asked Me, and I gave each person what they requested, My possessions would diminish only as the sea diminishes when a needle enters it.
My servants, I count your deeds and give you their recompense. Whoever finds good should praise Allah; whoever finds otherwise should blame only themselves.”

text: Narrated by Abu Dharr al-Ghifari, recorded in Sahih Muslim.
This lesson focuses on repeating imperative requests using the form "ask Me... and I will..." (e.g., استهدوني أهدكم). It presents highly structured parallel phrases.

source.translation:
Abu Dharr reported that some companions said to the Messenger of Allah: “Those with wealth have taken the rewards. They pray and fast as we do, and they also give charity from their extra wealth.”
He replied: “Has Allah not given you things with which to give charity? Each glorification of Allah is charity, each declaration of His greatness is charity, each expression of praise is charity, and each declaration of His oneness is charity. Encouraging good is charity, discouraging wrongdoing is charity, and sexual intimacy within marriage is charity.”
They asked whether fulfilling their desire could earn a reward. He asked: “If someone fulfilled it unlawfully, would they not be committing a sin? Likewise, fulfilling it lawfully earns a reward.”

text: This lesson explores Hadith 25 of Imam al-Nawawi, which broadens our understanding of "Sadaqah" (charity). We learn that physical wealth is not a constraint to performing acts of devotion and benevolence. Everyday goodness, praise, and sound conduct constitute vital, rewardable forms of charity.
"Every declaration of glory is a charity, every declaration of greatness is a charity..."

source.arabic: عن أبي هريرة رضي الله عنه قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «كل سلامى من الناس عليه صدقة، كل يوم تطلع فيه الشمس: تعدل بين اثنين صدقة، وتعين الرجل في دابته فتحمله عليها أو ترفع له عليها متاعه صدقة، والكلمة الطيبة صدقة، وبكل خطوة تمشيها إلى الصلاة صدقة، وتميط الأذى عن الطريق صدقة». رواه البخاري ومسلم.
source.translation:
Abu Hurayrah reported that the Messenger of Allah said:
“For every joint in a person's body, charity is due on each day the sun comes up. Bringing justice between two people is charity. Helping someone with their riding animal, by assisting them to mount or lifting their belongings onto it, is charity. A good word is charity. Each step taken towards prayer is charity. Taking something harmful off the road is charity.”

text: This lesson covers Hadith 26 of Al-Nawawi, demonstrating that charity is not limited to monetary giving, but extends to everyday acts of helpfulness, fairness, and positive social conduct.
Sahih al-Bukhari & Sahih Muslim (Hadith 26 in An-Nawawi's Forty Hadith)

In many cultures and legal traditions, charity is strictly defined as giving money or assets. However, Islamic terminology introduces a broader concept of physical and social charity.

source.arabic:
عَنِ النَّوَّاسِ بْنِ سَمْعَانَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ، عَنِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ قَالَ: "الْبِرُّ حُسْنُ الْخُلُقِ، وَالإِثْمُ مَا حَاكَ فِي نَفْسِكَ وَكَرِهْتَ أَنْ يَطَّلِعَ عَلَيْهِ النَّاسُ"

وَعَنْ وَابِصَةَ بْنِ مَعْبَدٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: أَتَيْتُ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فَقَالَ: "جِئْتَ تَسْأَلُ عَنِ الْبِرِّ؟" قُلْتُ: نَعَمْ. قَالَ: "اسْتَفْتِ قَلْبَكَ، الْبِرُّ مَا اطْمَأَنَّتْ إِلَيْهِ النَّفْسُ وَاطْمَأَنَّ إِلَيْهِ الْقَلْبُ، وَالإِثْمُ مَا حَاكَ فِي النَّفْسِ وَتَرَدَّدَ فِي الصَّدْرِ، وَإِنْ أَفْتَاكَ النَّاسُ وَأَفْتَوْكَ"
source.translation:

source.arabic: عن معاذ بن جبل رضي الله عنه قال: قلت يا رسول الله، أخبرني بعمل يدخلني الجنة ويباعدني من النار. قال: «لقد سألت عن عظيم، وإنه ليسير على من يسره الله عليه: تعبد الله لا تشرك به شيئا، وتقيم الصلاة، وتؤتي الزكاة، وتصوم رمضان، وتحج البيت». ثم قال: «ألا أدلك على أبواب الخير؟ الصوم جنة، والصدقة تطفئ الخطيئة كما يطفئ الماء النار، وصلاة الرجل في جوف الليل». ثم تلا: «تتجافى جنوبهم عن المضاجع» حتى بلغ «يعملون». ثم قال: «ألا أخبرك برأس الأمر وعموده وذروة سنامه؟» قلت: بلى يا رسول الله. قال: «رأس الأمر الإسلام، وعموده الصلاة، وذروة سنامه الجهاد». ثم قال: «ألا أخبرك بملاك ذلك كله؟» قلت: بلى يا نبي الله. فأخذ بلسانه وقال: «كف عليك هذا». قلت: يا نبي الله، وإنا لمؤاخذون بما نتكلم به؟ فقال: «ثكلتك أمك، وهل يكب الناس على وجوههم، أو قال على مناخرهم، إلا حصائد ألسنتهم؟» رواه الترمذي وقال: حديث حسن صحيح.
source.translation:
Muadh ibn Jabal said: I asked the Messenger of Allah to tell me of a deed that would admit me to Paradise and distance me from the Fire. He replied:
“You have asked about a great matter, but it is easy for someone whom Allah helps: worship Allah without associating anything with Him, establish prayer, give zakat, fast Ramadan, and make pilgrimage to the House.”
Then he said: “Let me show you the entrances to goodness: fasting is a shield, charity puts out sin as water puts out fire, and prayer during the middle of the night.” He then recited the verses beginning “Their sides leave their beds” through “what they used to do” (Qur'an 32:16–17).
He asked: “Shall I tell you the head of the matter, its pillar, and its highest point?” I said yes. He replied: “Its head is Islam, its pillar is prayer, and its highest point is jihad.”
He asked: “Shall I tell you what holds all of this together?” I said yes. Taking hold of his tongue, he said: “Keep this under control.” I asked whether we would be accountable for what we say. He replied with the Arabic expression “May your mother lose you, Muadh!” and asked whether anything throws people into the Fire on their faces—or their noses—except what their tongues have produced.

text: Neither Harm nor Return of Harm

Explore a foundational social principle on preventing damage, learn to build passive and restrictive statements using "neither... nor," and study constructive English tools for safe conflict resolution.
