What is the difference between starting harm and returning it?

Imagine a neighbor accidentally builds an overflow pipe that drips onto another neighbor's land. That is initiating a problem. If the affected neighbor retaliates by intentionally blocking the pipe to flood the builder's yard, that is returning harm.
"Is it ever right to answer a wrong act with another wrong act?" Modern language learning and general ethics suggest finding calm ways to resolve disputes.

text: Understand claimant and denier roles in disputes. Study the core rule of providing proof and taking oaths, and practice applying obligation structures like 'must' and 'have to' in everyday scenarios.

A Lost Pen in a Classroom

Imagine you find a premium pen on a classroom desk. Another student comes forward and says: "That belongs to me!" What would you expect them to show to prove it is theirs? A name written on it? A receipt? If they have nothing, can they just take it?
Why is it dangerous to let people take property simply because they claim it? What rules protect us from false statements?

What defines a fair market and true mutual respect?

In any community or marketplace, trust is built on fair practices. When sellers undercut each other unfairly or buyers manipulate prices, everyone suffers. Think about how mutual respect maintains peace both in business dealings and personal friendships.

Have you ever witnessed or experienced someone trying to artificially raise a price or speak ill of a competitor? How did that affect the trust within that environment? Same-level respect is essential.

source.arabic: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ عَنِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ قَالَ: "مَنْ نَفَّسَ عَنْ مُؤْمِنٍ كُرْبَةً مِنْ كُرَبِ الدُّنْيَا، نَفَّسَ اللهُ عَنْهُ كُرْبَةً مِنْ كُرَبِ يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ، وَمَنْ يَسَّرَ عَلَى مُعْسِرٍ، يَسَّرَ اللهُ عَلَيْهِ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ، وَمَنْ سَتَرَ مُسْلِمًا، سَتَرَهُ اللهُ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ، وَاللهُ فِي عَوْنِ الْعَبْدِ مَا كَانَ الْعَبْدُ فِي عَوْنِ أَخِيهِ، وَمَنْ سَلَكَ طَرِيقًا يَلْتَمِسُ فِيهِ عِلْمًا، سَهَّلَ اللهُ لَهُ بِهِ طَرِيقًا إِلَى الْجَنَّةِ، وَمَا اجْتَمَعَ قَوْمٌ فِي بَيْتٍ مِنْ بُيُوتِ اللهِ يَتْلُونَ كِتَابَ اللهِ وَيَتَدَارَسُونَهُ بَيْنَهُمْ، إِلَّا نَزَلَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ السَّكِينَةُ، وَغَشِيَتْهُمُ الرَّحْمَةُ وَحَفَّتْهُمُ الْمَلَائِكَةُ، وَذَكَرَهُمُ اللهُ فِيمَنْ عِنْدَهُ، وَمَنْ بَطَّأَ بِهِ عَمَلُهُ، لَمْ يُسْرِعْ بِهِ نَسَبُهُ."
source.translation: Whoever relieves a believer of some worldly distress, Allah will relieve him of some of the distress of the Day of Resurrection. And whoever makes things easy for those who are in difficulty, Allah will make things easy for him in this world and in the Next. And whoever shields a Muslim, Allah will shield him in this world and in the Next. Allah will aid His servant as long as the servant aids his brother. And whoever follows a path to seek knowledge, Allah will make easy for him a path to Paradise. No people gather in one of the houses of Allah, reciting the Book of Allah and studying it together, but tranquility descends upon them, mercy envelops them, angels surround them, and Allah mentions them to those near Him. And he whose deeds slow him down will not be hastened forward by his lineage.
source.citation: Source: Sahih Muslim · Hadith 36, Nawawi's Forty Hadith · sunnah.com/nawawi40/36

text: Analyze reciprocal whoever/will relationships in community support and study the language of service and mutual growth in clear B1 English.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Identify reciprocal 'whoever / will' logical structures in community context.
Explain and apply seven terms: relieve hardship, person in need, offer help, seek knowledge, study together, shield a fault, and actions not lineage.
Summarize service and learning themes clearly in modern English sentences.
Distinguish ethical privacy (shielding faults) from unsafe concealment of harm.
The Power of Mutual Help & Continuous Learning

How does community support function in your life? Think of a time you helped someone and how that action made things easier for the group. We are going to explore the logical links between human effort, divine assistance, and shared knowledge.
"Whoever does action X, God will provide outcome Y." This structure builds a chain of mutual support where your effort triggers safety and growth.
Quick Self-Assessment: How often do you participate in study groups?
You are on the second step of the lesson. Activate your thoughts to unlock the full Hadith text.
- shield a fault: cover private errors kindly
Listen to the high-quality recitation of Hadith 36. Pause or adjust pace as you read.

Notice the repeated conditional patterns:
- "Whoever relieves..." -> "Allah will relieve..."
- "Whoever makes things easy..." -> "Allah will make things easy..."
This structures a direct logical connection between our actions and divine results.
Review these five core B1 expressions, observing how their meanings match the specific context of Hadith 36.
To make a difficult situation less severe.
e.g., "Charitable micro-loans help struggling entrepreneurs relieve hardship during economic downturns."
Someone who requires help or essential resources.
e.g., "Community centers provide warm clothing and emergency meals to every person in need."
To say that you are willing to assist.
e.g., "Courteous coworkers proactively offer help when a teammate faces tight project deadlines."
To try to learn and understand.
e.g., "Scholars travel across the globe to seek knowledge in specialized archives."
To learn or review material with others.
e.g., "Medical students study together each evening to master complex surgical anatomy."
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
look into — examine, investigate, or research a subject with scholarly thoroughness.
pass on — transmit valuable knowledge, skills, or heritage to others.
useful knowledge — practical, beneficial insight that improves human well-being.
practical help — tangible assistance that resolves a concrete, immediate problem.
seek ≈ search for; find means to discover or encounter successfully
Not: He helped me to finding it. | Use: He helped me find it (help + object + bare infinitive).
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.
Determine how the B1 condition leads to the spiritual or worldly outcome based on Hadith 36.
"Whoever makes things easy for those in difficulty..."
CORRECT MATCH: Allah makes things easy in both worlds
Choose the correct B1 connector (to, in order to, because) to complete this sentence:
"They gather in the mosque [to / in order to] study the Book together."
In a balanced B1 setting, evaluate which scenario correctly follows BOTH the virtue of shielding private faults AND the duty of public safety:
An acquaintance makes a minor personal mistake. You counsel him privately to help him fix it, keeping his privacy intact.
A serious safety threat occurs in the community. You choose not to report it to keep the person's secret. (Warning: This violates public safety and mandatory reporting guidelines).
Describe Three Ways to Help & Learn
Practice presenting your thoughts aloud. Use the sentence frames to share three practical, safe ways to help others or seek knowledge in your daily neighborhood life.
"One way I can [offer help] is by [specific action]. This helps to [relieve hardship] for a neighbor."
"One way I can offer help is by tutoring a peer in English. This helps to relieve hardship for a student in difficulty, and we can study together."
Tap to record your 30-second explanation. We respect your privacy — audio is processed only locally.
Verify if your spoken answer contains:
Explain the reciprocal relationship between relieving distress and receiving aid.
Hint: Think about the 'whoever' clauses in the text.
Feedback: Helping a believer in worldly distress directly matches the outcome of Allah relieving our distress on the Day of Resurrection.
Why must shielding a fault never cover serious harm or crimes?
Hint: Think of the safety guardrails regarding abuse and justice.
Feedback: Protecting privacy applies only to small private errors. Legal, safety, or abuse threats must be reported to protect the community.
Arabic and English translations sourced directly from Sahih Muslim via Sunnah.com.

source.arabic: عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فيما يرويه عن ربه تبارك وتعالى قال: «إن الله كتب الحسنات والسيئات، ثم بين ذلك: فمن هم بحسنة فلم يعملها كتبها الله عنده حسنة كاملة، وإن هم بها فعملها كتبها الله عنده عشر حسنات إلى سبعمائة ضعف إلى أضعاف كثيرة. وإن هم بسيئة فلم يعملها كتبها الله عنده حسنة كاملة، وإن هم بها فعملها كتبها الله سيئة واحدة». رواه البخاري ومسلم.
source.translation:
Ibn Abbas reported that the Prophet related from his Lord:
“Allah has recorded good deeds and bad deeds, and has explained them. If someone intends a good deed without doing it, Allah records one complete good deed. If they intend it and do it, Allah records ten good deeds, up to seven hundred times and still more. If someone intends a bad deed without doing it, Allah records one complete good deed. If they intend it and do it, Allah records one bad deed.”
source.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari & Sahih Muslim · Hadith 37, Nawawi's Forty Hadith

text: Understand how sincere intentions are recorded by Allah even before an action is fully completed, and practice explaining intentions vs. completed achievements using B1 language.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Distinguish pure intentions (niyyah) from physical actions.
Identify the four distinct divine recorded outcomes of deeds.
Correctly explain and use 6 core curriculum terms.
Contrast intentions and completed actions using 'plan to' and 'manage to'.
Can different intentions guide identical visible behaviors?

Imagine two neighbors who both water an elderly relative’s garden. One helper does it with sincere gratitude and a hope to please Allah, while the other does it solely in order to receive a cash tip. Same action, completely distinct intentions.
We routinely separate internal plans from what we actually manage to achieve. In this lesson, we will see how Allah values and records these internal steps.
You are on the second step of the lesson. Activate your awareness of intentions before reading the full prophetic narration.
All practice scenarios in this curriculum use generic fictional examples of helpful or unhelpful deeds. We will never ask you to confess personal sins, errors, or private spiritual motives.
Listen to the standard Arabic pronunciation, synced with the English translation line by line.

Any specific legal, theological, or ultimate divine judgments regarding how rewards are calculated are subjects for advanced theological study and require qualified scholar (scholar) validation. Our focus here is solely B1 English language study of these structures.
Review these five core B1 expressions, observing how their meanings match the specific context of Hadith 37.
e.g., "I intend to volunteer at the civic medical center every weekend this semester."
To perform or complete a planned action.
e.g., "Project managers must carry out safety inspections before commissioning the plant."
A helpful or morally good action.
e.g., "Planting trees in urban neighborhoods is a lasting good deed that benefits future generations."
e.g., "Refraining from a wrong deed out of moral conviction earns immense spiritual reward."
e.g., "Recording angels write down every intention and action with absolute accuracy."
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
carry through — complete an undertaking successfully despite demanding obstacles.
hold back from — restrain oneself deliberately from committing a harmful action.
sincere intention — a genuine, unpretentious resolve formed purely for the sake of goodness.
recorded deed — an action formally documented in the eternal ledger of personal accountability.
deed ≈ action; deed often emphasizes moral quality and significance
Not: He intended of going. | Use: He intended to go ('intend' takes to-infinitive).
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.
Determine which part is the pure intention and which is the completed physical action. This requires zero personal confession.
"Faisal resolved to donate his old textbooks to a community library (Intention), and yesterday he dropped them off at the counter (Completed Action)."
Complete the B1 sentence matching intention with outcome:
"He planned to clear the garden path, but he couldn't find his tools. Today, he finally managed to do it with help."
Islamic teachings clearly distinguish between fleeting passing thoughts (which carry no responsibility) and settled intentions (which drive spiritual reward).
Contrast Planned Actions and Completed Deeds
Use the sentence frame below to explain what someone planned to do versus what they managed to complete. Keep your description safe and objective.
"He planned to [helpful intention], but he was interrupted. Later, he managed to carry out [good deed]."
"He planned to visit his sick neighbor on Monday, but he had to work late. Thankfully on Tuesday, he managed to carry out his visit and bring some food."
Did I use 'planned to' for intention?
Did I use 'managed to' for completed deed?
Did I avoid forced disclosure of private wrongs?
Contrast of Intention vs. Physical Completion
Model Statement: "While a settled intention (niyyah) starts the reward record, the physical act represents the completed execution of that motive."
Four Divine Outcomes Listed in Hadith 37
Outcome Checklist: (1) Intended good, not done. (2) Intended good, completed. (3) Intended bad, not done. (4) Intended bad, completed.
Hadith source extracted from sunnah.com/nawawi40/37 (Al-Bukhari & Muslim). Translation designed for standard B1 intermediate language teaching context.

source.arabic: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: "إِنَّ اللَّهَ قَالَ: مَنْ عَادَى لِي وَلِيًّا فَقَدْ آذَنْتُهُ بِالْحَرْبِ، وَمَا تَقَرَّبَ إِلَيَّ عَبْدِي بِشَيْءٍ أَحَبَّ إِلَيَّ مِمَّا افْتَرَضْتُ عَلَيْهِ، وَمَا يَزَالُ عَبْدِي يَتَقَرَّبُ إِلَيَّ بِالنَّوَافِلِ حَتَّى أُحِبَّهُ، فَإِذَا أَحْبَبْتُهُ كُنْتُ سَمْعَهُ الَّذِي يَسْمَعُ بِهِ، وَبَصَرَهُ الَّذِي يُبْصِرُ بِهِ، وَيَدَهُ الَّتِي يَبْطِشُ بِهَا، وَرِجْلَهُ الَّتِي يَمْشِي بِهَا، وَإِنْ سَأَلَنِي لَأُعْطِيَنَّهُ، وَلَئِنِ اسْتَعَاذَنِي لَأُعِيذَنَّهُ".
source.translation: On the authority of Abu Hurayrah (ra) who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah (mighty and sublime be He) said: Whosoever shows enmity to a friend (wali) of Mine, I shall be at war with him. My servant draws not near to Me with anything more loved by Me than the religious duties I have imposed upon him, and My servant continues to draw near to Me with voluntary deeds so that I shall love him. When I love him I am his hearing with which he hears, his seeing with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks. Were he to ask [something] of Me, I would surely give it to him, and were he to ask Me for refuge, I would surely grant him it."

text: Explore how required duties (must/have to) build the foundation of faith, and how optional habits (choose to) help us grow. Learn to discuss purpose and personal routines in correct English.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Distinguish between obligatory (required) duties and voluntary (optional) deeds.
Correctly sequence the core components of the narrative flow of Hadith 38.
Explain six natural English vocabulary terms in their appropriate context.
Use B1 target grammar (must/have to versus choose to/can) to compare habits.

In daily life, we divide our schedules into things we *must* do (paying bills, basic jobs) and things we *choose* to do to improve or build friendships (giving gifts, studying extra). Same structure applies to our spiritual path.
We start with required structures, then build beautiful extra habits around them. How do we express these differences naturally in B1 English?
How comfortable are you using words like "must," "have to," and "choose to" to talk about your daily routines?
You are activating background knowledge before engaging with the script text.
Understanding the structural differences of required duties ensures we communicate our daily habits with high accuracy. Next, we will read and listen to the core text.
Listen to classical Arabic pronunciation alongside correct English phrasing. Recommended speed: 1.0x.

Highlight where 'must' and 'choose to' are represented in the translation context. For example, "the religious duties I have imposed" maps to mandatory requirement, while "voluntary deeds" maps to free choice.

The phrases "I am his hearing... his seeing..." are respected as classical metaphorical descriptions of Divine support, guidance, and spiritual success. Precise interpretation of these expressions is left to qualified scholars.
Review these five core B1 expressions, observing how their meanings match the specific context of Hadith 38.
To act with hostility towards someone.
e.g., "Corrupt oppressors often show enmity toward human rights defenders."
In this narration, a close servant or friend of Allah.
e.g., "Classical texts describe a wali as one whose heart is devoted entirely to divine service."
To become closer; here, through worship.
e.g., "Seekers draw near to their Creator through quiet contemplation and regular worship."
An obligation required by religious guidance.
e.g., "Performing prescribed daily prayers is the most beloved religious duty."
An extra act of worship beyond what is required.
e.g., "Giving surplus charity and night prayers are voluntary deeds that elevate spiritual rank."
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
turn to — direct one's prayers, reliance, and petitions to God in time of need.
set aside — reserve a specific portion of time or wealth dedicated purely to devotion.
regular worship — consistent devotional practice maintained reliably day after day.
quiet reflection — peaceful, focused meditation on spiritual values and blessings.
devotion ≈ commitment; worship denotes sacred adoration directed toward the Creator
Not: He is devoted for worship. | Use: He is devoted to worship.
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.
Drag each daily task to its correct grammatical category based on necessity:
"going to bed on time" vs "reading extra chapters of study material"
Fill in the blank with 'must / have to' or 'choose to / can':
"In my work, I ________ attend weekly team standups, but I ________ read articles on weekends."
Reorder the words to construct a proper B1 English sentence:
draw / draw near / voluntary deeds / we / through

This course focuses purely on language acquisition. It never asks learners to claim a specific spiritual rank, measure their private sincere intentions, or declare divine love. These personal evaluations are private matters of faith.
Use the sentence frame below to compare a necessary duty in your profession or studies with a voluntary, helpful habit you choose to do.
"In my daily work, I **have to / must** [name a required task]. However, I also **choose to / can** [name an optional task] in order to draw near to my colleagues and learn new skills."
"In my daily studies, I **must** submit my assignments on time to pass. However, I also **choose to** read extra research articles in order to draw near to my goal of becoming an Islamic scholar."
Grammar Tip: Remember to use 'must' for absolute necessities.
Assessment Result: Pass. Language frames used correctly to describe obligations.
Completion represents active vocabulary study and B1 grammar structure comprehension only. Sincere motivation remains a personal journey.

source.arabic: "إِنَّ اللَّهَ تَجَاوَزَ لِي عَنْ أُمَّتِي الْخَطَأَ وَالنِّسْيَانَ وَمَا اسْتُكْرِهُوا عَلَيْهِ"
source.translation: Indeed, Allah has pardoned for my Ummah their mistakes, their forgetfulness, and what they are forced to do under duress.
source.citation: Source: Ibn Majah 2045 & al-Bayhaqi. Hasan (good) hadith.

text: Understand the three major circumstances of pardon in Islamic ethics, and learn to talk about accidental actions, forgetfulness, and forced decisions in clear English.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Distinguish clearly between mistakes, forgetfulness, and coercion.
Identify the three pardoned circumstances narrated in the Hadith.
Define and use 6 core B1 vocabulary terms accurately.
Construct sentences naturally using 'accidentally', 'forgot to', and 'was forced to'.
Imagine you are studying and drop your pen by mistake. Now imagine you drop it on purpose to get someone's attention. The physical action is identical, but the internal state is completely different.
Did you do anything accidentally, or forget a simple task? Understanding these everyday human situations prepares us for the grammar of excuse.
You are on the second step of the lesson. Complete this warm-up to unlock the exact Hadith text.
We will study these concepts in detail:
• Pardon: to excuse or overlook a mistake.
• Duress: when someone is forced to act against their will.
"Indeed, Allah has pardoned for my Ummah their mistakes, their forgetfulness, and what they are forced to do under duress."
This Hadith outlines how divine compassion protects people from moral blame in three conditions where clear thinking is absent.
Review these five core B1 expressions, observing how their meanings match the specific context of Hadith 39.
To forgive or excuse an offence.
e.g., "Just leaders pardon minor infractions when the offender demonstrates genuine remorse."
e.g., "Charities provide international humanitarian relief to members of the ummah and beyond."
An error in an action or decision.
e.g., "The junior clerk made an honest mistake when entering invoice figures."
e.g., "Lapses caused by genuine forgetfulness do not carry moral guilt or divine punishment."
To be made to do something against your will.
e.g., "A hostage may be forced to sign a false confession under physical duress."
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
mix up — confuse or mistake one item, person, or date for another accidentally.
move on — proceed forward constructively after experiencing an honest error.
honest mistake — an accidental blunder committed entirely without deceit or malice.
sudden pressure — acute, unforeseen stress or intimidation compelling an emergency reaction.
a mistake is an error; an accident is an unintended event, often one causing damage or injury
Not: I forgot to called. | Use: I forgot to call (forget + to-infinitive).
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.
Match the correct connector ('accidentally', 'forgot to', 'was forced to') to these everyday situations:
"I _________ call my colleague because my phone battery ran out."

If you or someone you know is in a dangerous situation, facing threats, coercion, or severe pressure, please seek support immediately from a trusted adult, family member, or local protection authorities. Do not handle dangerous duress alone.
Master the difference between deliberate and accidental outcomes. Read the sentence frames below and speak your own safe example out loud.
"I wanted to [intended plan], but I accidentally [unintentional action]. I am glad it is pardoned."
"I wanted to save my document, but I accidentally deleted it. It was a complete mistake."
1. Did I state a safe, everyday scenario?
2. Did I use the target connector 'accidentally'?
Identify the three major circumstances where moral blame is pardoned.
Model Answer: Mistake, forgetfulness, and what they are forced to do under duress.

source.arabic: عن ابن عمر رضي الله عنهما قال: أخذ رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بمنكبي وقال: «كن في الدنيا كأنك غريب أو عابر سبيل». وكان ابن عمر رضي الله عنهما يقول: إذا أمسيت فلا تنتظر الصباح، وإذا أصبحت فلا تنتظر المساء، وخذ من صحتك لمرضك، ومن حياتك لموتك. رواه البخاري.
source.translation:
"Be in this world as if you were a stranger or a traveler."

Ibn Umar added:
"In the evening do not expect to live until the morning, and in the morning do not expect to live until the evening. Take advantage of your health before your sickness, and your life before your death."

text: Explore the powerful metaphor of the traveler in Islamic thought. Learn how to discuss life goals, time planning, and healthy priorities in accurate English.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain the traveler metaphor in calm, daily context.
Logically sequence Ibn Umar's wisdom on organizing time.
Define and write sentences with 6 core B1 vocabulary terms.
Correctly apply 'before/after' and 'make use of' for healthy routines.
Packing Light for a Short Journey

When you go on a brief weekend trip, do you pack your entire wardrobe or only what is necessary? A wise traveler carries exactly what they need to reach their destination comfortably without being weighed down.
How do you organize your day to balance work, family, and personal growth? Thinking about priorities helps us understand the traveler's focus.
The Prophet (peace be upon him) suggests a wonderful frame of mind: living in this world with the gentle detachment of someone who is just passing through.
"Be in this world as if you were a stranger or a traveler."
This passage encourages us to focus on the value of today and preserve healthy opportunities.
Review these five core B1 expressions, observing how their meanings match the specific context of Hadith 40.
Someone unfamiliar or away from their own community.
e.g., "Traveling in a foreign metropolis makes you realize you are a temporary stranger."
A traveller passing through a place.
e.g., "The wise view this earthly life as a brief roadside rest for a journeying wayfarer."
To think that something will happen.
e.g., "Prudent people do not expect indefinite good fortune without taking practical precautions."
To make good use of an opportunity or resource.
e.g., "Ambitious students take advantage of library resources during the semester."
A person's physical and mental condition.
e.g., "Cherish your youth and robust health before illness and aging curtail your mobility."
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
set off — embark upon a meaningful journey or expedition with purpose.
move along — advance continuously along life's road without becoming entangled in distractions.
brief stay — a short, temporary period spent in a temporary location.
travel light — journey through life with few encumbering material possessions.
temporary ≠ brief; temporary describes non-permanent duration, while brief means short in time
Not: I am away since Monday. | Use: I have been away since Monday (use present perfect with since).
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.
Complete the sentence with the correct B1 terms related to daily routines:
"To build a strong mind and body, I should always _________ my morning energy _________ I start feeling tired."
Practice speaking about the lesson metaphor using simple English terms. Fill in the blanks out loud:
"A wise traveler focuses on reaching the destination. Similarly, I want to make use of my [healthy routines] and organize my time before [facing challenges / sickness]."
"A wise traveler focuses on reaching the destination. Similarly, I want to make use of my morning energy and organize my time before I feel tired."
1. Did I explain the traveler metaphor?
2. Did I use 'make use of' correctly?
Model Answer: We must live mindfully, packing only what is good, and making best use of health and time for positive priorities.

source.arabic: "لَا يُؤْمِنُ أَحَدُكُمْ حَتَّى يَكُونَ هَوَاهُ تَبَعًا لِمَا جِئْتُ بِهِ"
source.translation: None of you [truly] believes until his desire is subservient to what I have brought.

text: Understand Nawawi Hadith 41 and the B1-level concept of personal choice alignment. Explore the balance between private desires and trusted moral guidance. Learn how to describe value-driven actions in correct English.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Distinguish pure raw desires from guided choices.
Identify the grammatical conditions in the hadith sentence structure.
Define and explain 6 core B1 vocabulary terms correctly.
Properly use conditional conjunctions like "until" and "unless".

When navigating a complex city, you can explore on pure gut instinct or follow a reliable GPS device. Both options involve traveling, but following trusted guidance leads you to your destination safely.
Having personal desires is normal and healthy. The hadith does not paint desire itself as evil. Instead, it invites us to align our actions and choices with a trusted source of wisdom.
Think of personal desire as the engine of a car, and revelation as the steering wheel. The engine provides the initial power, but the steering wheel keeps the vehicle on the correct path.
"None of you [truly] believes until his desire is subservient to what I have brought."
"A sahih hadith which we have transmitted in Kitab al-Hujjah with a sahih chain of transmission."

To have sincere faith; the expression is used in the narration.
e.g., "To truly believe is to place ethical integrity above private financial gain."
e.g., "Unchecked personal desire must be disciplined by reason and revealed moral principles."
Following or subject to another authority.
e.g., "In an ethical professional, personal ambition remains subservient to public interest."
Advice or direction that helps someone choose a course of action.
e.g., "Seeking divine guidance through daily reflection anchors us during cultural storms."

Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
think through — evaluate all ethical implications of a decision before acting.
turn away from — consciously reject destructive impulses or unlawful temptations.
thoughtful choice — a carefully deliberated decision guided by moral reflection.
reliable guidance — authoritative direction from a proven, trustworthy mentor or scripture.

Not: a desire of success | Use: a desire for success (desire takes preposition 'for').

Read the scenario and choose the option that best models alignment with moral guidelines rather than pure, unguided impulse:

"Tariq is shopping at the marketplace. He finds an item he really likes, but realizes the seller made a mistake and undercharged him. Tariq's desire is to keep the extra money, but his ethical guidelines values fair trade."
A) Tariq ignores the mistake because he wants the product cheaper.
B) Tariq tells the seller about the mistake to align his actions with honest trade guidelines.

Practice speaking out loud about values and guidelines in English. Use the frame below:
"I want to make sure my personal [actions / desires] always [align with / follow] trusted moral guidelines."

source.arabic: "يَا ابْنِ آدَمَ إِنَّكَ مَا دَعَوْتَنِي وَرَجَوْتَنِي غَفَرْتُ لَكَ عَلَى مَا كَانَ فِيكَ وَلَا أُبَالِي، يَا ابْنَ آدَمَ لَوْ بَلَغَتْ ذُنُوبُكَ عَنَانَ السَّمَاءِ ثُمَّ اسْتَغْفَرْتَنِي غَفَرْتُ لَكَ وَلَا أُبَالِي، يَا ابْنَ آدَمَ إِنَّكَ لَوْ أَتَيْتَنِي بِقُرَابِ الْأَرْضِ خَطَايَا ثُمَّ لَقِيتَنِي لَا تُشْرِكُ بِي شَيْئًا لَأَتَيْتُكَ بِقُرَابِهَا مَغْفِرَةً"
source.translation: "O son of Adam, so long as you call upon Me and ask of Me, I shall forgive you for what you have done, and I shall not mind. O son of Adam, were your sins to reach the clouds of the sky and were you then to ask forgiveness of Me, I would forgive you. O son of Adam, were you to come to Me with sins nearly as great as the earth and were you then to face Me, ascribing no partner to Me, I would bring you forgiveness nearly as great as it."
source.citation: Reported in Jami` at-Tirmidhi (Hadith 3540). It is classified as a Hasan (good) hadith.

text: Explore the encouraging lessons of Hadith 42 at a B1 vocabulary level. Understand the balance between absolute hope in divine mercy and active moral responsibility. Learn how to express concepts of scale and condition in English.
By completing this lesson, you will learn to:
Identify three repeated divine promises of forgiveness.
Explain analogies of scale, such as 'sins reaching the clouds' and 'sins as great as the earth'.
Define and correctly use 6 core B1 vocabulary terms.
Express logical conditions using 'as long as', 'even if', and 'ask for forgiveness'.
Understand hope without compromising accountability, community safety, and ethical repair.

Imagine attempting to wash a very large shipping vessel or clearing a massive field. The sheer scale can feel overwhelming if we only rely on a small handheld brush. To achieve complete cleaning and restoration, we require a source of water and support that is proportionally vast.

Hadith 42 teaches that no matter how vast human shortcomings might seem—even reaching the clouds or matching the vastness of the earth—divine forgiveness is always greater, provided we turn back sincerely and maintain correct belief.

We balance absolute hope with active responsibility. Seeking forgiveness is a path to rectify our state, but it must be coupled with sincere efforts to repair mistakes, respect others, and maintain societal guidelines.

This beautiful narration offers tremendous hope and encouragement. At the B1 learning level, pay attention to the scale-based comparisons used to describe how expansive mercy can be when met with sincere intention.
Review these five core B1 expressions, observing how their meanings match the specific context of Hadith 42.
To call upon Allah in prayer.
e.g., "Humble believers invoke their Lord in private supplication during trials."
A wish and expectation that something good will happen.
e.g., "No matter how deep past mistakes, sincere hope in divine forgiveness must never waver."
To pardon a wrong or offence.
e.g., "The merciful nature of God is ready to forgive all who turn back with genuine repentance."
Actions that violate religious or moral guidance.
e.g., "Sincere repentance washes away accumulated sins and restores moral clarity."
A metaphor describing something extremely high or great in amount.
e.g., "Even if your accumulated errors were to reach the clouds in volume, divine mercy is vaster."
Language extension · Use these expressions to discuss the lesson theme in everyday English.
hold onto — maintain faith, hope, and determination firmly despite overwhelming adversity.
ask for — petition humbly and directly for pardon, assistance, and guidance.
hopeful outlook — a serene, confident expectation of future benevolence and redemption.
sincere prayer — a heartfelt, authentic petition uttered with genuine emotional devotion.
hope ≠ expect; hope expresses longing trust, while expect assumes certainty
Not: I hope you to forgive me. | Use: I hope you forgive me ('hope' takes a that-clause or to-infinitive for self).
Quick practice: Choose one phrasal verb and one collocation. Write or say one sentence for each.
Review the fictional scenario below. Identify the decision that reflects a balanced understanding of hope paired with responsibility (appropriate reporting, repair, and victim safety):

"Yusef accidentally damaged a client's property while setting up a workstation. Although he knows that mistakes can be forgiven ethically, his professional guidelines require protecting the client's interests."
A) Yusef hopes the client won't notice, reasoning that simple internal hope is sufficient.
B) Yusef immediately reports the damage, secures the site for safety, and offers to repair or replace the item.
C) Yusef leaves the location immediately to avoid any administrative accountability.
Practice explaining the balance between hope and responsibility in English. Try to use the following structure:
"Sincere hope is available [as long as / provided] we turn back with genuine regret, [even if] our mistakes seem major, but we must still work to make things right."
"Sincere hope is available as long as we turn back with genuine regret, even if our mistakes seem major, but we must still work to make things right in the community."
1. Did I state the condition using 'as long as' or 'even if'?
2. Did I include the aspect of ethical responsibility and repair?

Model Answer: Ethical restoration is fully open to whoever turns back sincerely and holds proper guidelines, regardless of the previous level of error, but active steps to repair harm remain essential.
